people.name: Renee Bowser
bio: Renee Bowser is a veteran labor leader and community activist who has been a devoted part of the WPFW listening family since the early 1990s. As a dedicated trade unionist, Renee spent her career fighting for workers to have a voice on the job, representing diverse employees in fields ranging from nursing to packinghouse work to secure better conditions and stable futures. Her lifelong commitment to justice has spanned from serving as an anti-discrimination investigator to organizing boycotts against corporations doing business with apartheid South Africa and working in the movement to free political prisoners.

Deeply rooted in local advocacy, Renee has served as a volunteer Advisory Neighborhood Commissioner and worked with Empower DC to champion safe, affordable housing and tutor unhoused children. At WPFW, she has been a vital leader for the station, volunteering on the Local Station Board for several years and serving as its chair.

In 2024, Renee brought her expertise to the airwaves as the host of Unionism Drives Community! Through her program, she explores the intertwined lives of the working class and promotes the intentional solidarity needed to advance the status of Black and Brown communities. Beyond her work in the studio, Renee remains active in public service as the Labor Member on the District of Columbia Public Employee Relations Board and continues her community organizing efforts with DC for Democracy.

eps.desc:
Skilled carpenters on publicly funded D.C. affordable housing projects were paid at unskilled laborer rates, and their employers falsified the payroll records to hide it. Sarah Bessel, supervisory counsel of the Washington Lawyers Committee for Civil Rights and Urban Affairs, walks host Renee Bowser through *A Rotten Foundation*, the committee's 2025 report covering a decade of federal and D.C. lawsuits and roughly 25 wage theft cases. Misclassifying workers as independent contractors strips them of overtime, prevailing wage rates, and workers' compensation. Bessel identifies employer threats of immigration action as a particular reason so few workers come forward.

The Washington Lawyers Committee runs a free Workers' Rights Clinic every Wednesday at 5 PM at Bread for the City Northwest on 7th Street in Shaw — phone 202-319-1000. Their recommendations to D.C. Council include a 5-times multiplier penalty for misclassification, a public wage theft database modeled on New York's, and better coordination between the D.C. Housing Production Trust Fund and the Office of the Attorney General's Workers' Rights Division.

Cedric DeLeon opens with a provocation: the empirical data, he argues, shows that Black workers — not white allies — were the primary architects of interracial solidarity in American unions. His new book *Freedom Train* presses that claim hard, even knowing it will unsettle labor studies circles. DeLeon brings organizer experience to the argument, having worked for the United Farm Workers, District 1199 SEIU, and the American Federation of Teachers between 1994 and 2006; he now teaches sociology and labor studies at the University of Massachusetts Amherst. From there he turns to a puzzle in the present: why record-high public approval of unions hasn't moved membership numbers. He points to employer misclassification of workers as independent contractors, automation, and the export of unionized jobs to the Global South. Host Renee draws him through the distinctions between social movement unionism, business unionism, and service unionism.

The conversation closes on a specific case. The 2017 UAW campaign at a majority-Black Nissan plant in Canton, Mississippi becomes a study in what happens when a union organizes for recognition without addressing the racial and social conditions workers face outside the plant gates — a limit, DeLeon suggests, that runs through the broader history *Freedom Train* sets out to tell.

Vicente Martinez spent eight years as a Starbucks barista in Denton, Texas, and qualified for company health insurance exactly once. Starbucks controls the scheduling that determines eligibility. Martinez and fellow bargaining delegate Jasmine Lolly of Buffalo, New York, join host Renee Bowser to explain why Starbucks Workers United has called a nationwide boycott, citing hundreds of alleged unfair labor practices and stores running five workers during peak hours instead of thirteen.

The union has also pressed to remove silica powder from blended-drink recipes after workers reported lung irritation. Still unresolved at the bargaining table: a $17 starting wage, guaranteed minimum staffing of three workers on the floor, and just-cause protections. The boycott pledge is at boycottstarbucks.net.

Ryan Marshall, organizer and Joint Apprenticeship Training Committee member of Ironworkers Local 5, opens with a striking promise: members who work thirty years can retire on a pension that pays more than their working wage, plus an annuity that may reach $1 million. The union's four-year apprenticeship requires only seventh-grade math and no high school diploma. Marshall's own credits include the Frederick Douglass Bridge, the Wharf, and the upcoming Commander Stadium. He also describes a federal Department of Labor investigation into a job site where non-union ironworkers were misclassified as independent contractors — a problem he says affects 23 percent of construction workers in Washington, D.C.

Host Renee Bowser closes with news from a different front: an arbitrator ruled in favor of Washington Post opinion journalist Karen Attia, finding she did not commit gross misconduct and rejecting the Post's attempt to hold her responsible for threats made against her by outside actors.

Nearly 40% of green jobs require a high school diploma or less — and those positions pay 8 to 9% more per hour than national averages. That is the research Devashree Saha, Director of the Clean Energy Economy Program at the World Resources Institute, brings to host Renee Bowser, drawing on Brookings Institution findings. Saha puts the global picture in sharp relief: 35 million clean energy jobs now exist worldwide, edging out 32 million in fossil fuels. In the United States alone, nearly 3.6 million clean energy jobs existed at the end of 2024, with energy efficiency holding the largest share, and over 60% of new utility-scale solar, wind, and battery manufacturing projects are sited in Republican congressional districts.

The numbers, though, only go so far. Saha argues that transportation, childcare, and what she calls "wraparound services" are the real barriers keeping lower-income workers from reaching training programs. She also warns against training workers too narrowly for technologies whose market demand can shift with policy changes.

Amazon spent $5 million trying to stop Chris Smalls from organizing JFK8 and deliberately churned workers at over 150% annual turnover to keep wages at entry level and block collective identity from forming. Renee Bowser of *Unionism Drives Community* walks through Smalls' book *When the Revolution Comes: A Fight for the Future of the Working Class*, tracing how the Amazon Labor Union prevailed anyway at the Staten Island warehouse. That same company, in 2025, was required to pay $3.95 million to the District of Columbia after the Office of the Attorney General found it had diverted customer tips meant for Amazon Flex delivery drivers to offset their base wages.

A caller working for a Washington, D.C. landscape company raises the legal bar on agricultural workers forming unions in D.C., Virginia, and Maryland. That question carries the conversation into Biden-era Department of Labor regulations that may extend some organizing protections to those workers.

Lynn Reinhardt, former General Counsel of the AFL-CIO and senior counselor to the Secretary of Labor in the Biden administration, has a pointed answer to the claim that project labor agreements drive up construction costs: labor is roughly 20–25% of total project costs, and efficiency gains offset higher wages. Now a senior fellow at the Economic Policy Institute, Reinhardt joins host Renee Bowser on *Unionism Drives Community* to explain how PLAs actually function on publicly subsidized projects like the RFK Stadium redevelopment, and why they are legally distinct from pre-hire agreements. The cost advantage non-union contractors hold on public bids — up to 30%, she argues — comes not from paying lower wages outright but from misclassifying workers as independent contractors.

Union hiring halls, which are legally required to refer qualified non-members, enter the conversation alongside what the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act provides for apprenticeship transportation and childcare subsidies. Bowser points to Ward 7 and Ward 8 residents, where unemployment runs into double digits, as a population still underconnected to building-trades apprenticeship pipelines.

people.name: Jim Byers
bio: Jim Byers is the long-time host and producer of Latin Flavor Classic Edition on WPFW, where he has been a mainstay of the airwaves for three decades. He first joined the station at age 28 after being invited by founding producer Hector Corporan and DJ Rhonda Shore, who were impressed by his extensive record collection and deep knowledge of Latin jazz. While he never originally planned on being an on-air personality, he saw the microphone as a unique opportunity to educate the public on the historical impact of the genre.

In his professional life beyond the booth, Jim recently retired as the Director of Marketing for the Arlington Cultural Affairs Division after more than 29 years of service. His career in the arts began in the late 1980s as a coordinator for the Charlin Jazz Society, where he curated and co-produced Global Rhythm, a week-long symposium held at venues like the Kennedy Center.

Jim describes his work as revolutionary radio, fueled by a belief that preserving history is a radical act in an era where community stories are often erased. Using his personal collection of over 20,000 records and pieces of memorabilia, he paints a musical portrait for his listeners, creating multiple access points for both novices and experts to engage with the music. One of his signature segments, "News According to Mambo," specifically connects vintage rhythms to the current events of the day. His expertise is so widely recognized that his program has been integrated into the History of Pop Music curriculum at both Boston College and Boston University.

Outside of his broadcasting and marketing work, Jim is a de facto neighborhood historian for his Southeast D.C. community, where he has led walking tours of Hillcrest and Penn Branch for over 20 years. He is also a documentary filmmaker currently working on a project about 1950s nightclub star Joyce Bryant. In his spare time, he is an avid vintage car enthusiast, with a collection centered on a rare 1971 Plymouth Sport Fury in Mood Indigo Iridescent.

eps.desc: Host Jim Byers devotes this birthday-eve edition of *Latin Flavor Classic Edition* to pianist Charlie Palmieri, revealing along the way that both Palmieri brothers studied under Margaret Bonds — the African American composer who kept studios at Carnegie Hall — and that it was Charlie, already a child prodigy, who brought his younger brother Eddie to her. Byers traces Palmieri's specific innovations: his Dubonnet Orchestra becoming the first commercially successful charanga in the U.S. around 1959, and his directing the Alegre All-Stars from 1961, whose extended descarga recordings — stretching to four, five, and six minutes at a time when radio formats demanded under four — helped set the stage for the modern salsa era. The two-hour program closes with unreleased 1953 RCA Victor studio sessions gifted to the show by the late producer Joe Conzo, including a version of "Este Es Mambo" with a passage never included on the released recording, alongside cuts featuring Palmieri alongside Tito Rodríguez, Tito Puente, Pupi Campo, and Pete Terriss.

Tito Puente leaned into someone's microphone at a 1979 live concert at World Trade Center Plaza and credited Stevie Wonder with pressuring NARAS behind the scenes to create the first Grammy categories for Latin music. Host Jim Byers built this September 11th edition of *Latin Flavor Classic Edition* around that recording, dedicating the show to historian Joe Conzo Sr. on what would have been his birthday — Conzo collected and curated the tape.

The episode also honors bassist Israel Cachao López on the eve of his birthday, with selections from *Cachao y su Descarga 77*, a midnight tribute session recorded after the death of Noro Morales on the Alegre label in 1964. A live recording of El Jamaiquino from the Palladium Ballroom in 1954 surfaces here too — remarkable because owner Max Hyman otherwise banned recording entirely. Byers traces Conzo's work across liner notes and reissues: a 1978 Arcáneo reissue of Tito Rodríguez's *Three Loves Have I* and the Columbia Legacy release of *The Original Latin Dance King*.

people.name: Lady C
bio: Christal Wooten, known to her listeners as Lady C, is a born-and-raised Washingtonian who brings the grown folk sounds of Southern Soul to the WPFW airwaves. A devoted member of the station family since 2012, she is a familiar and soothing voice for the DMV community.

Christal's journey at WPFW began as a co-host for Southern Soul Rumpin, where she worked alongside the late Doctor Nick for over 11 years. Following his retirement, she was referred to become the new host of the program, which has since evolved into The Southern Soul Party. Through this transition, she has remained dedicated to preserving the legacy of the show while making it her own.

Every Saturday, Lady C curates a high-energy noon day mix designed to get listeners moving, whether they are finishing their afternoon housework or relaxing under a shade tree. Her broadcasts feature a carefully selected blend of old and new school Southern Soul, blues, and R&B. She views the microphone as a tool for connection, speaking to her audience with a warmth and familiarity that makes them feel as though they are right there in the studio with her.

Christal is a firm advocate for authentic expression, guided by the personal mantra: "Everyone deserves to tell their own story." For Lady C, the most rewarding part of her work is the joy she brings to her audience. She finds deep fulfillment in meeting loyal listeners of 20 or 30 years at station events and hearing that her music and humor helped make their day a little brighter.

eps.desc: Lady C's Southern Soul Party on WPFW opened with a brief commentary on the Kennedy Center, where Lady C described protesters sharing memories of seeing their first musical and first orchestra there, and argued that listeners should vote in November to change the political direction. The rest of the hour was a deep playlist of southern soul, featuring tracks by artists including Aretha Franklin, Marvin Gaye, James Brown, Tyrone Davis, Denise LaSalle, Omar Cunningham, Tucker, and Jeter Jones, several of whom Lady C noted were performing that same day at American Legion Post 170 in Indian Head, Maryland; she also paused mid-show to announce the passing of her uncle, Edward Jones Sr., and to celebrate birthdays and anniversaries called in by listeners.

I'm gonna sing pretty for the people," says Jessie Terrell, a Chicago-born singer who has called Washington home for 17 years. Her forthcoming album *After Hours* is built around intimate love songs, and on September 19th she heads to Indian Head, Maryland for an outdoor show headlined by Karen Wolfe, J Redd, and Jeter Jones.

Mid-show, Ray Apollo Allen calls in with a story about years performing alongside Solomon Burke — "we called him Saul" — and marks his 60th year in the music business with a birthday set that afternoon at Bistro 64 on Marlboro Pike. The music on Lady C's Southern Soul Party ranges from J. Morris Group, Vic Allen, Mr. Breeze Too Much, and Marvin Gaye to the Teskey Brothers.

people.name: Ellen Williams Carter
bio: Ellen Williams Carter is the host of Morning Brew — Jazz Notes Edition, a program she has curated since 1986. A cornerstone of the WPFW community, Ellen has been a devoted listener since the station's founding in 1977 and began her service as a volunteer in 1986. Beyond the microphone, she serves the station in a critical governance role as the Secretary of the WPFW Local Station Board.

eps.desc:
Lakecia Benjamin knew Alice Coltrane's music before she ever heard John Coltrane's — and that imbalance drove her to make *Pursuance: The Coltranes*. The album was recorded after a car accident so severe that, as Ellen Carter puts it, survival seemed unimaginable. In a 2024 interview with Carter, Benjamin says she wanted to "equal the playing field" between them.

Carter hosts this two-hour segment of WPFW's all-day John Coltrane centennial tribute, threading Coltrane's spiritual and romantic sides through selections that span his full career: his first recorded solo with Dizzy Gillespie's band on March 1, 1951; the *A Love Supreme* quartet sides with McCoy Tyner, Jimmy Garrison, and Elvin Jones; a 1956 session with Kenny Drew and Philly Joe Jones. A local Washington ensemble closes the block with Coltrane's "Equinox.

eps.t: Morning Brew Jazz Notes Edition feat. Union City Radio
eps.desc:
Slam Stewart could play arco bass while simultaneously singing the same line an octave higher. Ellen Carter plays him in a September 21 birthday salute, noting she once interviewed him and introduced him at a concert. Her two-hour *Morning Brew Jazz Notes Edition* builds around John Coltrane's centennial, moving from Lakecia Benjamin's *Pursuance: The Coltranes* with Dee Dee Bridgewater on vocals through Alice Coltrane's *Translinear Light* to Branford Marsalis and Dianne Reeves' tribute album *Dedicated to You*.

Stewart is not the only birthday being marked on September 21. Henry Butler, a pianist and composer born that date in 1948 and blinded by glaucoma as an infant, gets his own spotlight. A Labor Radio Podcast Daily segment rounds out the programme, marking the 1913 date when Mother Jones led a march of miners' children through Charleston, West Virginia.

eps.desc:
As a child, Ellen Carter sneaked fast food into Nat Adderley's house in Teaneck — that's where they first encountered Cannonball Adderley, born September 15, 1928. The episode also marks the birth anniversaries of Joseph Jarman (September 14, 1937) — AACM co-founder, Shinshu Buddhist priest, and Army paratrooper injured in a Vietnam raid that killed 18 U.S. soldiers — and organist Jack McDuff (September 17), who gave George Benson his first break.

From there the story turns to Charlie Byrd, who carried bossa nova recordings by João Gilberto and Antônio Carlos Jobim back from Brazil and played them for Stan Getz at his home. The two recorded *Jazz Samba* live at Pierce Hall at All Souls Unitarian Church in Washington, D.C. in 1962. It closes with liner notes in which Byrd, plagued by chronic respiratory difficulties near the end of his life, told a writer over breakfast: "I'm not used to looking back.

people.name: Eugenia Charles
bio: Eugenia Charles is the Host and Executive Producer of Konbit Lakay, WPFW 89.3 FM’s long-running Haitian public affairs, socio-political, and cultural program. A dedicated political analyst and community organizer, Eugenia uses her platform to promote informed dialogue on immigration, human rights, and issues affecting underserved communities. Her commitment to the airwaves is guided by the mantra, "Education is Power," as she strives to provide an independent platform where overlooked voices can discuss complex issues with depth and honesty.

Eugenia’s journey with WPFW began in 2001, and she joined the Konbit Lakay team in 2002 to help educate listeners about the Haitian diaspora. She stepped into her current leadership role in 2017, continuing the program's more than 40-year legacy of public service. Beyond the studio, she serves as the Executive Director of Fondasyon Mapou and is a co-editor of the book Let Haiti Live: Unjust U.S. Policies Towards Its Oldest Neighbor.

Her dedication to advocacy and legal analysis is furthered by her pursuit of a Juris Doctor degree. Eugenia’s service to the community has been recognized with the "Haiti Freedom for All" plaque, honoring her outstanding contributions to the Haitian people's struggle for democracy. Through Konbit Lakay, she continues to educate and empower listeners across the Washington metropolitan region and beyond.

eps.desc:
Haitian diaspora radio program *Konbit Lakay*, hosted by Eugenia Charles, spends most of the hour examining Trump's nomination of Austin Holmes as the next U.S. ambassador to Haiti. Charles draws on Holmes's own February 10, 2026 Senate Appropriations Committee testimony, in which he disclosed that in 2003 he established a specialized security company to support kidnapping negotiations in Haiti and has since led a coalition of over 600 NGOs and partner organizations there. She questions whether a figure who spent 17 years running NGOs and then formed a private security firm is suited for the role, comparing his trajectory to that of Erik Prince, who she says holds a contract worth over $50 million and uses drones that have killed Haitian civilians.

The program also takes up the end of TPS and Senate bill S.4814, which would extend protected status for over 350,000 Haitians for three years. Deportation flights have been landing in Cap-Haïtien after the airport's 4 PM closing time. The International Organization for Migration reports the displacement of more than 10,000 people in Kerskoff. And a new Miami federal charge has been brought against Rafael Guerrero of Pembroke Pines in connection with the assassination of former President Jovenel Moïse.

Caroline, a communal representative from Kenscoff's second communal section, counted at least 46 bodies with her own eyes after the August 23rd massacre. She tells host Eugenia Charles that local officials had already warned police about threats before the attack, yet nothing was done. She adds that gang members are holding more than 50 people hostage as leverage against government action.

Charles also plays an excerpt from a recent *Haiti on Our Mind* session with Jean Saint-Ville, known as Jafrik Afrika, a Pan-Africanist author based in Canada, who argues that Haitian fighters at the 1779 Battle of Savannah were children used as cannon fodder, not volunteers — a history he connects to the current UN-sanctioned multinational security force in Haiti. The episode also covers ICE's arrest of 1,328 people from Maryland and Virginia in the first two weeks of August; the release of Haitian businessman Dimitri Vob after more than 300 days in immigration detention; and Haiti's under-14 national soccer team winning the 2026 CFU Challenge Series.

Eugenia Charles had been Yvon Florival's agent for years, first meeting him when he designed sets for Théâtre Mapou productions, including a staging of a Jacques Roumain play. Florival died August 25, 2026, at 72. He had won a 1992 Congressional Black Caucus Spouse Quincy Jones Award and shown work at the White House Eisenhower Executive Building, the National Museum of American History, and the French Embassy in Washington. Charles devotes much of this episode of *Konbit Lakay* to his life and career.

She also follows the case of Pierre Damas Belle, a recent high school graduate and JROTC member in Springfield, Ohio, who was fitted with an ICE ankle bracelet during his first week of college and fell into depression — his father holds government immigration policy responsible. From there, Charles walks Haitian community members through concrete steps: finding a licensed immigration attorney before a crisis, understanding the new public charge test taking effect September 18th, and seeking mental health support. USCIS will now review credit reports as part of green card applications.

Caroline, a communal representative for the second section of Banga, told interviewer Woody Sanon she personally counted at least 46 bodies after the August 23rd massacre in Kenscoff, Haiti — a figure that excluded victims who died outside homes or went missing. She also told Sanon that local officials had warned police inspector Cadet that Kenscoff was at serious risk before the attack, yet no preventive action was taken. At a recent *Haiti on Our Mind* event at Sankofa, Pan-Africanist writer Jean-Séville Jafrik Afrika argued that the 1779 Battle of Savannah sent African captives — including a 12-year-old Henri Christophe — as cannon fodder, and drew a direct line from that history to Kenyan and Rwandan troops currently deployed to Haiti under UN mandate.

The programme's news segments move from that context to developments closer to the present: Haiti's under-14 boys soccer team winning the 2026 CFU Challenge Series in Punta Cana; businessman Dimitri Vob's release after more than 300 days in immigration detention; a federal judge's invalidation of the Trump administration's visa ban affecting 75 countries, including Haiti; and ICE's arrest of 1,328 people across Maryland and Virginia in the first two weeks of August. Eugenia Charles hosts.

Haiti is heading toward a December 13th election with roughly 104 political parties already in the certification process, and the CEP is pressing them to merge into coalitions. To help secure the vote, a Japan–OAS cooperation agreement delivers a $3 million grant to expand Haiti's national identification system and procure 350,000 blank biometric cards before the election.

Host Eugenia Charles tracks six Haitian and Haitian American candidates on Florida's primary ballot, among them Florida State Representative Doty Joseph seeking the Democratic gubernatorial nomination and physician Dr. Rudolph Moïse running in District 24 to succeed retiring Congresswoman Frederica Wilson. A recorded segment from Ezuli Danto on the 1791 Bois-Caïman gathering opens a broader discussion of what democracy and freedom mean under Haiti's current government. Charles argues that Prime Minister Alix Didier Filsaime has lost more territory to gangs than existed before he took office and is paying over $35,000 a month in legal fees to stay in power.

Eugenia Charles opens by arguing that the Bois-Caïman gathering of 1791 was not primarily a spiritual ceremony but a strategic political meeting — one that took twelve years to organize, carried out underground by women and men traveling routes unknown to slave masters in Saint-Domingue. That reframing anchors the anniversary episode of Konbit Lakay. The second half airs a segment from a WBAI special report on the TPS crisis, including New York Mayor Mamdani's statement explaining that the city was forced to separate Haitian municipal workers after the Supreme Court's 6-3 decision lifted a stay on ending TPS for 350,000 Haitians. Civil rights attorney Norman Siegel joins other guests to debate whether the city's move will trigger a cascading compliance effect across both the public and private sectors.

Viles Dorsainville, executive director of the Haitian Support Center in Springfield, Ohio, has watched TPS holders get summoned to ICE offices in Cincinnati and Westerville, fitted with ankle monitors, and offered $2,600 — money he says he has never seen anyone actually receive. Getting to those appointments is itself a problem: Springfield has no public transportation connecting it to either city, and TPS termination has stripped many holders of the ability to drive legally, leaving hundreds of community members dependent on others just to show up. Dorsainville, himself a plaintiff in a Northern California TPS case, tells host Eugenia Charles what that looks like on the ground.

The Haitian Support Center he now leads grew out of a specific moment of loss — it was founded in the aftermath of the 2023 school-bus accident that killed 11-year-old Aiden Clark. Dorsainville also raises two pieces of pending legislation: S.4814, which would extend TPS by three years, and S.2106, both of which listeners can bring to their representatives.

At a July 21st congressional hearing, Ambassador Michael Kozak could not confirm the State Department was consulted before DHS Secretary Noem terminated Temporary Protected Status for over 350,000 Haitians. The termination took legal effect July 27th, after the Supreme Court's June 25th ruling returned the case to Judge Ana Reyes. Host Eugenia Charles plays that audio, which features questioning by Representatives Gabe Amo and Gregory Meeks. She then turns to House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast's description of the Kenya-led security mission as "an ineffective boondoggle," countering that the U.S. drafted the resolution creating it, brokered Kenya's participation through IMF and World Bank access, and still owes Kenya unpaid funds.

The program also covers a congressional delegation's July 27th visit to Haiti and a newly published electoral calendar scheduling a first-round presidential vote for December 13, 2026. Listeners are given a phone number to call their senators in support of Senate Bill S.4814, which would extend TPS for three years.

people.name: Tom Cole
bio: Tom Cole is a veteran of the D.C. media landscape and a cornerstone of the WPFW family, having been a programmer with the station since its very first year in 1977. A second-generation Washingtonian and a proud graduate of the District's public school system, Tom's career in broadcasting spans several decades and includes significant roles at some of the nation's most prominent public media outlets.

Tom's journey behind the board began at the age of 24, when he started as a volunteer engineer for a children's program and a blues show. After he submitted a proposal for his own music program, Denise Oliver awarded him a Sunday morning slot and named the show G-Strings, a program Tom has hosted and produced ever since. He is also a keeper of the station's unique history, recalling the early, creative days when studios were separated by sheets hung on strings and the doorbell was a bucket of rocks attached to a window string.

Through G-Strings, Tom focuses on the beauty of stringed instruments, primarily the guitar, to showcase the deep connections between different peoples and cultures. His program is driven by a belief that music has a universal ability to unite us and that public radio should serve as a vital alternative to the mainstream. He finds great joy in introducing listeners to unfamiliar traditions and sharing music they may have never heard before.

Beyond his decades at WPFW, Tom's professional resume includes nearly ten years at WAMU as a board operator and Production Manager, three years as a producer for Voice of America, and a distinguished 33-year career as an editor and producer for NPR's Cultural Programming and News Divisions. Outside of the studio, he remains dedicated to his D.C. roots, volunteering his time during the school year to tutor students in reading.

eps.desc:
Red Mitchell was born September 20, 1927, in New York City, and Tom Cole's *G Strings* follows his career from West Coast sessions with Hampton Hawes all the way to Stockholm, where he settled in 1968. Chico Hamilton shares the birthday. The program draws on the *Sweet Smell of Success* soundtrack — actor Marty Milner's on-screen guitar fingerings were actually performed by John Pisano.

Sue Mingus gave one of her late husband's basses to Hungarian bassist Aladar Pégé after hearing him at the 1980 Jazz Yatra Festival in Bombay. The hour reaches toward the approaching Coltrane centennial through his 1958 session with Kenny Burrell, with violin from Billy Bang and the String Trio of New York, and bassist David Shevin's Afro-Semitic Experience. Miyuki Williams joins to discuss the upcoming WPFW Jazz and Justice Festival at Meridian Hill Malcolm X Park.

Butch Warren grew up in Washington, D.C., became the go-to bassist for Blue Note Records in the late 1950s and early 1960s, then spent decades struggling with addiction and mental illness. On his Sunday morning program G-Strings, Tom Cole traces him through two Grant Green sessions — one with Herbie Hancock, one with Sonny Clark, the pianist who first brought Warren to Blue Note's attention. Victor Dvoshkin's "Song for Edward," written for Edward Cohen, the man who helped Dvoshkin emigrate from the Soviet Union "at a fraught time," draws a pointed parallel to the present.

The three-hour program is anchored by a benefit concert that afternoon at Palisades Hub, featuring Herman Burney's group Two Bass Hit and Baltimore bassist Chris Funn's group Corner Store.

people.name: Chris Garlock
bio: Chris Garlock is a veteran labor communicator who brings the art and soul of the American labor movement to WPFW as the co-host of the Labor Heritage Power Hour. Every Thursday at 1 p.m., Chris and co-host Elise Bryant use the airwaves to celebrate the cultural heritage of workers, blending labor history with arts and culture.

Beyond his work in the studio, Chris serves as the Executive Director of the Labor Heritage Foundation. He is a driving force behind the annual DC Labor FilmFest, one of the few film festivals in the world dedicated to labor themes, and serves as a coordinator for both the Global Labor FilmFest Network and the Labor Radio Podcast Network.

Chris is also a prolific producer of digital content, helping to keep labor history alive through podcasts such as Labor History Today, Labor Radio Podcast Daily, and Labor Radio Podcast Weekly. His deep roots in the movement include previous service as the Union Cities/Street Heat Coordinator for the Metro Washington Council, AFL-CIO.

With an extensive background as a labor communicator across both print and radio, Chris remains dedicated to amplifying the voices and stories of the working class. He invites the WPFW community to join him in exploring the songs, stories, and struggles that define the American worker.

eps.desc:
Jane Fonda spent a long night with about 40 members of the Cleveland chapter of 9 to 5, asking what they'd dreamed of doing to their bosses. Karen Nussbaum, co-founder of the labor-feminist organization, explains how nearly every incident in the 1980 film came out of that conversation — including the woman ordered to sew a tear in her boss's pants while he was wearing them.

Popular and mass culture critic Cathy Newman and producer Lisa Rae Garlock discuss Vince Gilligan's series *Pluribus*, in which 13 people remain unaffected by a virus that makes everyone else cooperate without friction or conflict. What that premise reveals, they argue, is the invisible labor behind the delivery economy, immigration, and the cost of erasing individuality. Labor historian Peter Ratcliffe and author John Hanson then close the hour on *Fight and Win*, Hanson's account of the 1934 Minneapolis Teamsters strike. At its center is his father, a rank-and-file worker elected to the strike's democratic Committee of 100, and the person-to-person communications network that held the movement together.

UAW president Sean Fain stood in Tabitha Arnold's studio, pointed to a figure in the bottom right of her tapestry, and said "that's what I did" — recognizing himself from his time working in Kokomo. Arnold spent 224 hours weaving that piece for Volkswagen workers during their union drive, the first successful unionization of an auto plant in the South, and brought it to rallies before the vote so factory workers could see themselves memorialized on the production line. That same instinct — art as witness to labor — runs through the rest of the hour. At the 10th Reuther Pollock Symposium in Wheeling, West Virginia, artist Eric Ruanne credited his father's union pension — paid out after his death — as what allowed him to quit his first job and pursue art.

In Tacoma, Chris Garlock hears from former Pierce County Central Labor Council president Vance Lely, who explains how the annual Labor Day commemoration at Ralph Chaplin's grave grew from one activist's solitary vigil into a gathering of 60 union members. From there, Tampa DSA organizers Roger Butterfield and Manny Ramirez walk through Ybor City's labor history, including a 1937 march of roughly 5,000 women on City Hall to protest the bombing of Guernica — led to a mayor named Robert E. Lee Chancey.

Detroit's riverfront holds North America's largest public artwork dedicated to organized labor: *Transcending*, 63 feet of steel arches, bronze reliefs, and workers' quotations. Michigan Labor History Society guides John Dick and Dave Elsila walk Chris Garlock and his listeners through it in this episode of *Labor Heritage Power Hour*. From there, Dick turns to Hitsville, USA, where Freddie Gorman — a Detroit letter carrier and part-time songwriter — supplied the hook that turned Berry Gordy's unfinished song into "Please Mr. Postman," Motown's first number one hit. Gorman was then edged out of the Holland-Dozier-Gorman songwriting team and returned to carrying mail until retirement.

Harvard historian Kelly Goodman picks up the thread of Detroit labor history by tracing the teachers' 43-day strike of 1973, which began on Labor Day in resistance to merit pay and the automation of classroom work, through to the Chicago Teachers Union strikes of 2012 and 2019, and on to a 2022 Massachusetts ballot initiative that imposed a 4% surtax on incomes above $1 million to fund free community college and restore education cuts. The hour closes with singer and activist Hallie Hammer, who names "Union Maid" as her favorite labor song for putting union women at the center of the fight.

David Sherba's factory in Brunswick, Ohio, has built between 4,000 and 5,000 Scabby the Rats since the first one was made on May 4, 1992. Host Chris Garlock visits Inflatable Images to hear how the process shifted from hand-airbrushing — three or four days per rat — to digital printing and computer patterning.

Carmen Rodriguez interviews historian Eladio Bobadilla about his book *Dangerous Migration*, which documents how the UFW under Cesar Chavez turned undocumented workers over to the Border Patrol and ran its own border enforcement operation. Bobadilla connects the fear-based narratives used against immigrants today to a pattern reaching back to Benjamin Franklin's warnings about Germans. Pete Seeger performing "The Preacher and the Slave" in 1960 opens a listener-request hour marking the 115th anniversary of the IWW's Little Red Songbook — 38 editions between 1909 and 2010, with a 39th now in progress. Host Chris Garlock also airs Labor Heritage Foundation co-founder Saul Schneiderman singing an a cappella "Dump the Bosses Off Your Back." The hour's centerpiece is labor historian Nick Jurevich interviewing veteran organizer Phil Cohen about his memoir *Maximum Leverage: From the Street to the Picket Line*. Cohen drove illegal gypsy cabs in New York at 17, lived in a Skid Row hotel while clearing a stack of arrest warrants, and eventually rebuilt union locals from 30% to 80% membership. Among the tactics he describes: having workers fan out down separate aisles of a Sam's Club simultaneously so managers couldn't stop them all at once.

The labor arts news rounds out the hour. Video game workers rallied in six states against Xbox layoffs, the Traverse City Philharmonic voted to join the American Federation of Musicians, and workers ratified a first contract at Dallas Black Dance Theatre.

A 10-year-old Matt Damon lived next door to Howard Zinn in Boston, heard him typing *A People's History of the United States* through the wall, then went to school and argued Columbus was a monster — citing eyewitness Bartolomé de las Casas. The labor arts news segment reports Graham Nash and Jesse Wells canceling concerts at Richmond's Lewis Ginter Botanical Garden over a labor dispute, special effects workers across the Star Wars franchise organizing with IATSE, and the opening of *Woody Guthrie's American Song* in Washington, D.C.

Karsi Blanton accepted an award at Folk Alliance without a guitar and told the room she'd gone from $80,000 in debt at her last attendance to over $200,000 in debt a decade later. That speech anchors the final segment of this *Labor Heritage Power Hour*, hosted by Chris Garlock and Elise Bryant.

Before that, physician-songwriter Mindy Murray tells the Labor John podcast how her father's childhood farm labor near Morrisville, Pennsylvania drove her to write "Striking at Kings" — a song about the 1938 King Farm strike, where workers earned as little as 17 cents an hour. Labor journalist Kim Kelly sits down with J. Albert Mann to discuss her young-readers book *Fight to Win*, moving from Lucy Parsons to a trans autoworker named Joni Christian, and making the case that workers have organized under worse conditions than today's.

people.name: Craig Hall
programs: Brother Ah's Collectors: Next Generation in Sound
bio: Craig Hall is a Pan-Africanist, family man, and dedicated lover of African music and culture who co-hosts Brother Ah's Collectors: Next Generation in Sound on WPFW. A long-time listener and supporter of the station before joining as a volunteer, Craig's journey behind the mic began when he was invited as a guest by the late Robert "Brother Ah" Northern. Following Brother Ah's illness, Craig further developed his broadcasting and technical skills by joining the program Voices With Vision alongside his long-time friend and comrade, Netfa Freeman.

Today, Craig is committed to carrying forward the legacy of Brother Ah by curating jazz music that reflects spiritually higher values and deep connections to African culture. His work is driven by a desire to advance WPFW's Jazz and Justice mission, blending exceptional music with a radical political perspective. Craig views his role as a "Scientist of Sound" dedicated to providing programming that cuts through the noise of commercial media to help the community emancipate itself from mental slavery. Through his broadcasts, he strives to provide a message of hope and progress while keeping the spirit of truth-telling alive on the airwaves.

eps.t: Brother Ah’s Collectors: Next Generation in Sound
eps.desc:
John Coltrane would have turned 100 on September 23rd. Brother Craig opens this tribute on **Brother Ah's Collectors: Next Generation in Sound** with "All or Nothing at All" from *Ballads*, and the dedications stack up from there: Khalil El-Zabar's version of "Resolution" with Isaiah Collier on reeds, then Bob Thiele's "Lament for John Coltrane" featuring Elvin Jones on drums. Coltrane's own "Song of the Underground Railroad" from *Africa Brass Volume 2* draws a note from Brother Craig — it features "our very own brother" Bob Northern on French horn.

The hour rounds out with the WPFW Jazz Calendar, local listings that run from Herb Scott at Yours Cafe in Georgetown to Isaiah Collier performing a Coltrane tribute at Keystone Corner in Baltimore.

eps.t: Brother Ah’s Collectors: Next Generation in Sound
eps.desc:
Brother Craig calls out the full personnel before every track — Kenny Kirkland on electric piano behind Carlos Garnett, Larry Carlton alongside Joe Sample on the Crusaders cut — treating the credits as part of the music. This is an all-1976 hour of *Brother Oz Collector's Next Generation in Sound*, fifty years on from the recordings. people.name: Daman Harris
bio: Dr. Daman Harris is an educator, author, and nonprofit leader who brings a deep commitment to expanding educational opportunities to the WPFW airwaves. As a collective member and host of #UMustLearn, he helps lead one of the DMV's most trusted sources for conversations on liberatory education, equity, and social justice.

Beyond the studio, Dr. Harris is a driving force in educational reform. He is the co-founder and co-director of The BOND Project and leads Capacity Education, LLC, working with schools and organizations to develop practices that improve outcomes for students and communities. A nationally recognized expert in his field, he is also the author of the book The Antiracist School Leader: What to Know, Say, and Do.

Daman's connection to the station began in 2022 when he moved from being a guest on #UMustLearn to a fill-in host, eventually joining the permanent hosting collective. He is motivated by the belief that education is one of the most powerful tools for strengthening communities and views WPFW as a vital platform for amplifying voices that deserve to be heard. Through his work on the air, he aims to provide listeners with practical insights and thoughtful dialogue that move beyond the headlines to inspire real-world action.

Daman lives by a clear personal mantra: "Learn deeply. Lead courageously. Leave every community stronger than you found it." He encourages the WPFW family to stay curious and engaged, advising listeners to seek out perspectives that challenge their own and to remember that their voice matters.

eps.t: Jam Session - Beats, Bars, and Bangers
eps.desc: Kamau Harris and co-host Science air this midnight-to-2am edition of *Beats, Bars, and Bangers* on what would have been John Coltrane's 100th birthday, September 23rd. Every track they spin samples Coltrane: Killer Priest pulling from "My Little Brown Book," Mac Miller and Schoolboy Q both drawing from "In a Sentimental Mood" (1963), Schoolboy Q and Freddie Gibbs sampling "Naima" (1960). From there the set moves into a Midwest hip-hop retrospective with cuts from Common, Chance the Rapper, Wu-Tang, and Eminem. The back stretch goes jazz-forward through Digable Planets and De La Soul — Digable Planets' Doodlebug attended Howard University in the mid-1980s. The episode closes with a preview of the following week's Blue-Eyed Soul session and details on the Jazz and Justice Festival at Malcolm X Park.
eps.prog: Jam Session - Beats, Bars, and Bangers

eps.desc: In 1957, Louis Armstrong publicly condemned the federal government's failure to protect the Little Rock Nine and refused a State Department tour in protest — and host Daman Harris opens this episode of *You Must Learn* by connecting that refusal to the 1963 bombing of the 16th Street Baptist Church, which killed four Black girls. New co-host Amy Watkins, a children's author, wrote a character with albinism after a student in her classroom had the condition. Tara Liebert of Free Minds Book Club — founded at the dying request of Glenn McGinnis, executed in 2000 at age 17 after writing from death row to ask for a book club for incarcerated youth — walks through the organization's Read for Youth Justice reading list, including its section on children with incarcerated parents. Richard Rogers, a principal leadership coach three weeks into his role at Prince George's County Public Schools, reflects on 33 years in education and being repeatedly assigned to high-need schools as a Black man on the assumption he could "wave a magic wand," while being denied the option of leading more affluent ones.

eps.t: Jam Session - Beats, Bars, and Bangers
eps.desc:
Kanye West was born in Atlanta and raised in Chicago — neither Kamau Harris nor co-host Science knew that before researching the show. They spend two hours on *Beats, Bars, and Bangers* working through hip-hop from all 12 Midwest states, and Harris adds another relocation story to the mix: Eminem was born in St. Joseph, Missouri before moving to Detroit.

The set moves from Slum Village and Kid Cudi to the Ohio Players, pulling in artists from Detroit, Chicago, Cleveland, and Cincinnati along the way, and closes on tracks sampled by RZA and J Dilla. Harris and Science sign off with shoutouts to listeners streaming live from North Carolina, the Bay Area, Florida, Atlanta, and Texas.
eps.prog: Jam Session - Beats, Bars, and Bangers

eps.desc:
A 65-year-old Black man can be biologically closer to 68 — not by calendar, but by what Dr. Tali Elliott called "sustained high-intensity trauma" and a "weathering effect" that accumulates over a lifetime. Dr. Jeffrey Johnson, coordinator of Black Men's Health at the African American Health Program, explained this to host Dr. Daryl Howard, alongside the stark gap: average life expectancy of 70.8 years for Black men versus 75.8 for white men. Johnson traced the Tuskegee Experiment's lasting grip on medical mistrust, then described his program's strategy of taking health screenings into barbershops, salons, and basketball courts, with a free Community Ambassador Training set for Saturday, 9 a.m. to noon.

That work of meeting people where they are finds a parallel in the history Kim Bishop and Troy Bishop bring to the program. They tell the story of Good Hope Union UMC in Colesville, Montgomery County — founded in 1870 by three freed Black farmers, John Powell, Tom Stewart, and Sam Jones, who bought the land from Sarah Watts. The congregation has counted the first ordained African American female pastor in the Baltimore-Washington Conference of the United Methodist Church and a Negro Leagues pitcher who played with the Newark Eagles, Birmingham Black Barons, and Atlanta Black Crackers. The Bishops describe plans to restore the 1913 sanctuary, ring its bell again, and host a free community health bazaar on September 19th.

Vaughn Bennett, a DC firefighter turned chess instructor, says the DC Chess League excluded Black DC residents from tournaments, scholarships, and leadership for nearly 80 years — a history the US Chess Federation documented in a 2022 report. Bennett has taught more than 7,000 children across 25 years. Baba Oso, a founding member of Kankuran West African Dance and Music Company, traces the banning of the drum under slavery to its role as a communication and healing tool, and previews the group's 43rd-anniversary performance at Crampton Auditorium at Howard University. Natani Victoria Lim of Embracing Equity, an Albuquerque-based nonprofit, describes its virtual workshops on building cultures of belonging in schools and a debate over whether to strip equity-related language from its website under current political pressure — a debate the team resolved by keeping the name and the mission intact. This episode of *#YouMustLearn* airs Thursday, September 3, 2026.

Toussaint L'Ouverture was lured to a meeting under a false promise of safety, captured, and left to die — and a lieutenant "a little over 20" finished the revolution and declared Haitian independence in 1804. Dr. Daryl Howard opens *#YouMustLearn* with that account before welcoming Baba Ayize and Dr. Azoma Miller, a professor of African American Studies at Ohio University, to discuss a Black August webinar they are co-hosting through the Asen of Kemet, an African-centered fraternity founded at Morehouse as an alternative to the Divine Nine. The two argue that George Jackson, Assata Shakur, and Fred Hampton are largely absent from mainstream education. Ongoing efforts to remove exhibits about George Washington enslaving Africans at his Philadelphia house, they contend, make erasure active, not passive.

That conversation about what gets left out gives way to a look at what Words, Beats & Life is building on the ground. Mwiza Munthali, executive director of the nearly 25-year-old hip-hop nonprofit, describes their upcoming Game Day — a free intergenerational event built around chess, checkers, dominoes, Uno, spades, mahjong, and video games. This summer was the first since 2020 when young people in their programs told staff they had made friends with kids from other neighborhoods they had never met.

Andre Kearns can trace his family to Emmanuel and Joan Cumbo — captives from the Kingdom of Ndongo in present-day Angola who arrived at Port Comfort around 1628 — and to his third great-grandfather William B. Harvell, sold as a child named Buck in an 1832 bill of sale. After emancipation, Harvell became a landowner, founded a church, and established a school that launched five generations of HBCU attendance in Kearns's family, with a sixth generation now at Howard. Kearns, a Washington D.C. native, genealogist, and author, sits down with the #YouMustLearn program on WPFW to tell that story.

The episode also turns to the DiverseCITY Fund's fall grant cycle, open to Black and brown-led organizations with budgets under $50,999 that do organizing, advocacy, or healing justice work in D.C. Board member Nkechi Feaster — who first encountered the fund while living in a family shelter at D.C. General — explains how its community grantmaking model deliberately removes the barriers that typically block impacted residents from both funding decisions and funding itself. Rounding out the hour, holistic health practitioner and Black Love Day founder Mama Ayo Handy Kendi previews WPFW's 5th annual 5K walk/run on September 12th at Bladensburg Waterfront Park, describing new additions that include walking meditation and strength training.

Cliff, co-founder of Blue Montessori on Marion Barry Avenue in Anacostia, teaches 3-to-6-year-olds using go-go drumming and HBCU-style marching. He argues that Montessori's emphasis on self-direction maps directly onto the demands of college and the workplace. His tuition-free school is in its third year.

Baba Ayize's #YouMustLearn turns next to film director Ime Atuk, whose film *Outdoor School* centers on a 12-year-old boy in 1994 Portland, Oregon living under a tree with his mother and sister while guarding a pair of neon Deion Sanders patent leather Nike shoes. After audiences at screenings were repeatedly affected by the film's treatment of domestic violence, Atuk began distributing a resource guide on the subject. He also recounts meeting a 12-year-old boy outside a theater in Ashland, Oregon whose family turned out to be in a situation mirroring the film's story. *Outdoor School* screens August 15th at the George Washington University Student Center as part of the ADIFF DC festival.

Curtis Valentine's great-grandfather co-founded a Rosenwald School; his book *Real Men Teach* traces that lineage back to John Chavis, a free Black man who taught white students in the early 1800s whose student went on to become a U.S. Senator from North Carolina. Valentine, founding president of the Male Educator Network and Policy Institute, joins host Daman Harris on *You Must Learn* at WPFW, with testimony from former students of Black male educators including U.S. Senator Raphael Warnock and Governor Deval Patrick, and a discussion of figures such as Charles Ogletree. 

Baba Clifton of Mommy's TLC announces a pre-celebration at 2616 Georgia Avenue Northwest on August 1st, marking 25 years and over 16,000 children served through the out-of-school-time program. Dr. Sekou Africa of Bowie State University describes building a pipeline for Black male educators from 8th grade through master's degree level, and explains how symptoms he mistook for a stroke and a heart attack shaped his new initiative, the Black Male Educator Classroom.

people.name: Daryl Howard
bio: Dr. Daryl Howard is a lifelong educator, author, and professor who serves as a collective member and host for the radio program #UMustLearn on WPFW 89.3 FM. A volunteer programmer with the station for the past two years, he contributes to weekly conversations designed to inform, inspire, and ignite the community through the lens of liberatory education.

Dr. Howard's professional expertise and advocacy are deeply rooted in race and cultural proficiency, social-emotional learning, and generational trends in technology. He is particularly dedicated to exploring and amplifying the experiences of male teachers and students within educational spaces, bringing these essential perspectives to the DMV community. Through his work on the airwaves, he helps provide a trusted platform for diverse voices to explore issues of equity and social justice.

Beyond his role as a broadcaster, Dr. Howard continues his extensive work as a professor and researcher, focusing on creating more inclusive and effective education systems. Listeners can tune in to hear Dr. Howard and the #UMustLearn collective most Thursdays at 6 p.m.
For more information on his professional work and research, visit darylhowardphd.com or connect with him on social media @darylhowardphd.

people.name: Willard Jenkins
bio: Willard Jenkins has spent his working life uplifting jazz — as a broadcaster, a writer, a festival director, and an advocate. He came to Washington in 1989 to serve as executive director of the former National Jazz Service Organization, and word reached WPFW that someone new in town had jazz radio experience. Tom Porter, then the station's general manager and program director, invited him down to the studios at 7th and H Streets NW in Chinatown. Like most programmers in that era, Willard signed up as a substitute, did some subbing, and gradually grew into a program of his own. He has been on the WPFW air since October 1989.

Over those decades he has held afternoon drivetime, morning drivetime, and the 10-to-midnight slot before settling into Sunday afternoons with Open Sky. The program is built on a simple split: the first hour is the classic side of the music, and the second is "What's New," devoted to contemporary and recent releases. He engages listeners by playing compelling music and speaking to it with a degree of lived authority.

Willard grew up in Cleveland and is a proud graduate of Kent State University, where his interest in public media began as part of a Black student movement that pushed for, among other things, a Black student newspaper on campus. That is where he started writing about jazz. The work carried him to the Cleveland Plain Dealer and then to jazz and arts publications around the world. He has broadcast at WWOZ in New Orleans, KFAI in Minneapolis-St. Paul, WKSU at Kent State, and WABQ and WERE in Cleveland, nearly all of it as an unpaid volunteer, and spent ten years with the former BET Jazz Channel developing and hosting programming including a weekly show devoted to jazz education. He founded the Northeast Ohio Jazz Society and spent eighteen years as artistic director of Tri-C JazzFest Cleveland. Since 2015 he has served as Artistic Director of the DC Jazz Festival.

He is the author of two books published by Duke University Press: African Rhythms in 2010 and Ain't But a Few of Us: Black Music Writers Tell Their Story in 2022, which was named Book of the Year About Jazz by the Jazz Journalists Association. The JJA gave him its Lifetime Achievement Award in 2013. In 2024 he received the National Endowment for the Arts Jazz Masters A.B. Spellman Award for Jazz Advocacy and an honorary doctorate from Kent State. More of his work is at openskyjazz.com.

eps.desc:
Willard Jenkins, NEA Jazz Master, anchors a two-hour centennial block on WPFW marking John Coltrane's September 23rd, 1926 birthdate. Drawing on the 1995 box set *The Heavyweight Champion: The Complete John Coltrane Atlantic Recordings*, he traces Coltrane's Atlantic years through "Giant Steps," "Naima," "Equinox," "Mr. P.C.," and a recording of Coltrane playing Ornette Coleman's "The Blessing" with Coleman's own rhythm section. A 1962 *DownBeat* interview surfaces in which Coltrane names Sonny Rollins as a favorite — pointed timing, given that Rollins had just been memorialized at the Cathedral of St. John the Divine. Program director Katea Stitt joins throughout to take pledges and discuss the Coltrane estate's vinyl box sets offered as premiums.

The block closes with a preview from incoming host Candy Shannon, whose following segment is built around interviews with specific people about their favorite Coltrane track and why.

Willard Jenkins calls Cassandra Wilson's *Blue Skies* one of his desert island discs, and he plays tracks from it — with Mulgrew Miller, Lonnie Plaxico, and Terri Lyne Carrington — alongside *After the Beginning Again* and *New Moon Daughter* in tribute to the recently deceased singer. Randy Weston's centennial falls on April 6th. Jenkins marks it with "The African Cookbook" from *Spirits of Our Ancestors*, featuring Pharoah Sanders, Dewey Redmond, and Billy Harper on tenor saxophones, played in memory of Weston's late wife Fatou.

The second hour opens a new-release segment with 2026 DC Jazz Pre-Bands Competition winner Luther Allison performing Harold Mabern's "There But for the Grace Of." From there the hour moves through George Benson's *Inspiration: A Tribute to Nat King Cole*, Joe Lovano's Paramount Quartet, DMV-based flutist Alex Hamburger, and Brazilian-born pianist José Luiz Martins. Big Chief Donald Harrison closes the segment with *The Magic Touch* — nine versions of one tune across styles including nouveau swing and bossa nova.

Willard Jenkins opens this edition of *Open Sky* by honoring jazz centenarians of 2026, spinning Oscar Brown Jr.'s "But I Was Cool" from *Sin and Soul*, Jack McDuff's "Rock Candy" with Houston Person on tenor, and a Miles Davis–Coltrane sextet reading of Thelonious Monk's "Straight No Chaser." The 3 o'clock new-release hour brings a Ledisi–Gregory Porter duet on Dinah Washington's "You've Got What It Takes," from Ledisi's tribute album *For Dinah*, then Jason Moran's solo piano take on Duke Ellington's "Fleurette Africaine" from *Jason Moran Plays Duke Ellington*. His wife Alicia Hall Moran follows with "River" — both records on the couple's YES Records label.

Jenkins also previews that afternoon's WPFW benefit concert at Palisades Hub, with tracks from the two headlining acts: Baltimore bassist Chris Funn's Corner Store and Herman Burney's Two Bass Hit. Rounding out the hour are a Gary Bartz medley by the Baltimore Jazz Collective and a set from Luther Allison, winner of the previous week's D.C. Jazz Pre-Emerging Bands Competition.

people.name: Saïs Kamalidiin
bio: Saïs Kamalidiin is a musician for life and educator who brings a deep, global perspective to the WPFW airwaves as the host of Jam Session ~ Life Music. A veteran of the station family, Saïs first joined the WPFW team in 1984 at the age of 34. He fondly remembers being greeted at the original H Street studio by Mr. Fish Middleton, whose warm welcome led to a six-year tenure as an on-air programmer.

After a hiatus to earn his doctorate in ethnomusicology, Saïs was invited back to the station in 2019. In his professional life beyond the booth, he has served as an Associate Professor of Music at Howard University for 27 years. He views independent community radio as an indispensable tool for navigating the complexities of modern life, drawn to the platform by the diverse range of opinions and viewpoints it allows.

On his program, Saïs provides a 360-degree exposure to the most potent musical traditions in existence, blending genres such as Jazz, Latin, Classical, and Folk. Guided by the mantra "Music is the healing force of the universe," he views WPFW programmers as "Scientists of Sound" who are mathematically laying it down on behalf of the community. He purposefully keeps his broadcasts unpredictable, never informing listeners what to expect next week to ensure each show is something completely different and of the highest quality.

Saïs is a firm advocate for intellectual autonomy and cultural freedom, especially as he observes the increasing gentrification of the District. He believes it is essential for the community to be knowledgeable about the full spectrum of global musical contributions. His advice to the WPFW family, and particularly to younger listeners, is to never stop seeking greater levels of wisdom and understanding, and to find like-minded companions to join them on that journey.

eps.desc: Saïs Kamalidiin marked John Coltrane's 100th birthday with an overnight hour he called "Kamala Dean's Coltrane Cooldown," programming the Gerald Wilson Big Band's "Equinox" alongside Ernie Watts and Mulgrew Miller performing "Lush Life" with flutist Hubert Laws, and "Afro Blue" from *Rise*. *Life Music* airs Thursdays from midnight to 2 AM on WPFW 89.3 FM.

Every music that is labeled American music ultimately starts in our community." That observation, from Saïs Kamalidiin, closed the episode.

Most of this late-night *Life Music* was given over to a full album presentation of Shaboozy's *The Outlaw Sherry Lee and Other Western Tales*, a cinematic concept record that follows a woman named Sherry Lee hunting down the men responsible for her father's death. Duke Pearson's "Prairie Dog" was among the other music aired. The programme had a timely backdrop: Kamalidiin noted that the Bill Pickett Invitational Championship Finals Rodeo was taking place that weekend at the Showplace Arena in Upper Marlboro, Maryland.

Saiïs Kamalidiin calls it a visit to "a bygone era," and the phones light up with memories, "some good, some not so good." TV theme songs anchor the hour — *A Different World*, *Living Single*, *Sister Sister*, *Chico and the Man* — alongside a dedicated set for pianist Wynton Kelly. The show runs midnight to 2 a.m. on this Thursday, September 10, 2026 edition of Life Music, before Kamalidiin hands the overnight to DJ Valentine.

Fidel Castro's centennial birthday prompted WPFW to run a full 24-hour tribute to Cuba, and Saiz Kamaluddin opened it at midnight with this special edition of *Life Music*. The playlist ran from Celia Cruz and Tito Puente to Orquesta Revé, Harry Belafonte, the Fania All-Stars, Pancho Sanchez, and Johnny Pacheco, with Pérez Prado's "Patricia" in the mix alongside Kenny Dorham's "Aphrodisiac" from his album *Afro-Cuban*. Between sets, Kamaluddin told listeners that later in the day they would hear stories, information about current conditions in Cuba, and ways to help. The broadcast ran from midnight to 2 a.m.

people.name: DJ Machete
bio: Jevon Howard, known to his listeners as DJ Machete, is a veteran programmer who brings the history and heart of Hip Hop to the WPFW airwaves. As the host of Decipher, airing every 4th Saturday, Jevon focuses on Golden Era Hip Hop and the art of the original sample. His program is designed not just to entertain, but to educate, introducing listeners to the source material that built the genre and encouraging them to become fans of the original artists who paved the way.

Jevon's journey with the station began in 2005 as part of the initial team for The Lab Hip Hop Show, which originally aired every Friday. Over his nearly two decades with WPFW, he has remained dedicated to sharing the kind of authentic music that commercial radio often ignores. While he is now a seasoned broadcaster, he fondly remembers the nerves he felt during one of his greatest highlights: the honor of opening for and hosting the legendary Grand Wizard Theodore during a live Friday night broadcast.

Beyond the studio, Jevon serves the DMV community through his professional career in HVAC for a local school district. In his spare time, he is a true student of sound, constantly collecting and listening to records to find the next great discovery for his audience.

Guided by a personal commitment to advance the culture, Jevon encourages the WPFW family to look beyond what is popular or trending. His advice to listeners is to always stay curious and be willing to navigate outside the box to find the profound wisdom and creativity that independent radio has to offer.

eps.desc:
DJ Senpai pulled up to DreamCon and found a black SUV waiting with his name on it — the kind of moment that should feel like arrival. The 36-year-old DC-area DJ told Eddie Smith, Ron Brown, and DJ Machete on Decipher that it took a therapist to help him work through the imposter syndrome and self-sabotage that followed. The conversation kept returning to money: DJs hauling $1,500 to $2,500 or more in equipment, maintaining flash drives, laptops, and backup gear across 17 years of learning to read a room cannot work for $200 or $300.

Longtime station supporter Marvin called in to argue that a DJ also has to know the racial and social justice issues of the community they serve. Noodles closed by announcing the Jazz and Justice Festival — Sunday, September 27th, noon to seven, at Malcolm X Park at 16th and Euclid Street Northwest — marking the park's 90th anniversary.

Bush Head Ed opened this Soul Controller Second Saturdays edition of *The Cypher* with a tribute to Peter Cullen — the voice of Optimus Prime — playing Big Daddy Kane's "Smooth Operator," with its line "transforming on stage like a Decepticon," alongside Gnarls Barkley's "Transformer" and Ty's "When Robots Go to War." Cullen had voiced the character from *Transformers*' 1984 cartoon debut through a forthcoming short film marking the franchise's 40th anniversary.

A Virgo-season birthday run covered Nas, Eazy-E, Doug E. Fresh, and Ludacris. Ed had caught Reese performing the 25th anniversary of *How I Do* at Songbird and followed that with her "Ice King" featuring Nas. Rapsody's "Pick a Side" from *God's Got an Afro and Gold Hoops* appeared alongside a posse cut from Storm the Unpredictable, Poor Righteous Teachers, Common and Pete Rock, and material from Nas and DJ Premier's "Pause Tapes" project. Ed broadcast the whole show after flying back from Alabama A&M on a 6 AM flight he nearly missed.

people.name: Warren "Scooter" Magruder
bio: Warren "Scooter" Magruder is a D.C. native and a lifelong lover of radio, R&B, and baseball who brings his passion to the airwaves as the host of Don't Forget the Blues. A veteran of the local music scene, Scooter has been a party street DJ since 1973 and a prominent voice on DMV radio since 1988. He officially joined the WPFW family in 2006 at the age of 58 after being invited by the station's Program Director to share his craft with the community.

On his program, Scooter uses a signature style of storytelling to guide listeners through the history of vintage R&B and the blues. He views his work as a way to honor the remembrance of Black America's original music and show how those roots paved the way for almost every other style of American music we enjoy today. Whether he is spinning records or hosting Community Watch and Comment, his goal is always to provide news you can use and a message of hope. He lives by a simple mantra: let the musical memories set the mood.

Off the air, Scooter is a dedicated community activist. He is deeply involved in social justice causes, including advocating for Palestinian rights, and is committed to mentoring young people in both broadcasting and essential life skills like reading. For Scooter, WPFW is a vital space to keep the truth alive and use the power of music and information to strengthen the community.

eps.desc:
T-Bone Walker wrote and recorded "Stormy Monday" first — Scooter Magruder makes sure listeners know that before the set is over. The September 17, 2026 edition of *Don't Forget the Blues* opens with a three-song Walker block, then moves through ZZ Hill, Bobby Parker, Blues Boy Willie, the Canes from the Stax box set, Dinah Washington, Ann Peebles with the Willie Mitchell Band, and Bobby Rush.

Elliott Gross reads a live blues calendar covering venues from Falls Church, Virginia to Harpers Ferry, West Virginia. The episode closes with notice of an upcoming 20th Blue Monday Blues anniversary and a farewell to Reverend Brian Hamilton at Westminster Church in Southwest DC.

James Brown once said that in the 1970s, only two artists stayed true to the blues: B.B. King and Bobby Blue Bland. On this episode of *Don't Forget the Blues* on WPFW 89.3 FM, host Scooter Magruder pairs their songs throughout the hour as a birthday tribute to Riley B. King. Elliott Gross reads the live blues calendar, listing upcoming performances at Leisure World in Silver Spring, the 219 Restaurant in Alexandria, and Westminster Church in Southwest DC. Magruder closes with birthday shout-outs to listeners in Fort Lincoln and Fort Washington.

people.name: Brother Jamil Muhammad
bio: Brother Jamil Muhammad is a dedicated voice on WPFW and the host of Morning Brew — Yardbird Sweets Edition. A staple of the WPFW family since the station's founding year of 1977, he transitioned from a long-time listener and donor to a prominent on-air personality. Every Tuesday morning, Jamil strives to provide his audience with an "ear full of music, a mind full of thoughts, and a heart full of joy," aiming to make listeners smile and dance their way to the bus stop.

Jamil's journey behind the microphone began at age 56 when he had the opportunity to co-host with the late Askia Muhammad. Guided by the principles and spirit of his radio elder, he remains committed to the station's mission of spreading "Jazz, Justice, and Joy." He is particularly passionate about the future of the airwaves, seeing WPFW as a vital space where younger Washingtonians can find a place of expression and receive training in the methods of community outreach.

Beyond the studio, Brother Jamil has served as a Muslim cleric for nearly five decades, a role that fills him with gratitude each day. Known affectionately as "Pop Pops" by his twelve grandchildren, he enjoys spending his spare time collecting jazz records and tinkering with his grandchildren's gadgets. His deep roots with the station, dating back to the era of Petey Greene, reflect a lifelong commitment to serving as a guardian of freedom and liberation for the community.

eps.t: Morning Brew Yardbird Sweets Edition feat. Union City Radio
eps.desc:
Arthur McLeod, sitting in for Bro Jamil, opens with a week's worth of birthdays: Gary Bartz, Marlena Shaw's "Woman of the Ghetto," and a Ray Charles set that moves from "What'd I Say" into a live-at-Montreux "A Song for You." McLeod notes that John Coltrane and Ray Charles share a September 23rd birthday.

Eddie Bo's "Hook and Sling," recorded live in New Orleans in 1999, sits alongside Les McCann and Eddie Harris at the Montreal Jazz Festival in 1969. The final hour shifts to what McLeod calls "black lights, strobe lights, basement" music — house parties lit by construction-site flashing yellow lights — and closes on Rare Earth's "Get Ready" and Mandrill's "Mango Meat.
eps.prog: Morning Brew Yardbird Sweets Edition feat. Union City Radio

eps.t: Morning Brew Yardbird Sweets Edition feat. Union City Radio
eps.desc:
Brother Jamil opens by dedicating Cannonball Adderley's "Serenata," from *Cannonball Takes Charge*, to Addie Mae Collins, Cynthia Wesley, Carol Robertson, and Denise McNair — the four girls killed in the 16th Street Baptist Church bombing on September 15, 1963, 63 years earlier. From the Askia Corner, a segment honoring *Morning Brew*'s late founder Askia Muhammad, he reads Claude McKay's "If We Must Die," a poem from McKay's 1890 birth year.

The rest of the programme turns on September birth anniversaries. Cannonball Adderley, born in Tampa, Florida in 1928, shares the occasion with Ray Charles, Sonny Rollins, and New York trumpeter Bruce Harris, who just turned 47; cuts come from Rollins's *Alfie* score, Samara Joy's *Portrait*, and Harris's *Soundview* and *Beginnings*. A Labor Radio Podcast insert marks the date in 1845 when some 5,000 women cotton workers in the Pittsburgh area struck for a ten-hour workday. New artist Ekepnkwele gets a spotlight ahead of her debut album *Early One Morning*, due the following month.
