people.name: David Rabin
bio: David Rabin is a dedicated public affairs programmer at WPFW who believes in building a better world, one broadcast at a time. A long-time member of the station family, David's connection to 89.3 FM began in the mid-1990s while he was working for Pacifica Network News, which was housed in the same building as WPFW. He fondly remembers his first direct contact with the station being Askia Muhammad, WPFW's beloved News Director, who would walk through the PNN offices passing out birthday cake to the staff.

David eventually transitioned from a neighbor in the building to an on-air personality, starting as a substitute host for several programs before establishing his own show. Over the years, he has become known for his compelling and high-impact interviews with figures who have shaped American history and advocacy. Some of his most memorable broadcasts have featured conversations with consumer advocate Ralph Nader, Tuskegee Airman Charles McGee, and Freedom Rider Charles Person. He has also used his program to explore deep systemic issues, such as discussing the history of enforced racial segregation with author Richard Rothstein.

Driven by a passion for community service, David views his role as a way to provide listeners with essential information that they might not find in mainstream media. He remains committed to using the power of the microphone to inform, support, and strengthen the community he serves.

eps.desc:
Kristen Civiletto's father developed radiation-linked cancer, and tracing its cause led her to uncover that Niagara Falls factories participated in steps of the Manhattan Project and dumped radioactive and chemical waste across the city for over 130 years. She tells host David Rabin that the waste is still migrating into homes today. An attorney and former Niagara Falls resident, she brought litigation on behalf of 1,500 families that was dismissed after 14 years on a preemption argument. Her forthcoming book is *Thundering Waters: The Toxic Legacy of Niagara Falls*.

The contamination she describes is not abstract. Jocelyn McKernan found industrial slag, graphite, and metal rods while digging a backyard pool 300 feet from Love Canal; her soil tests came back at 24 times the EPA lead standard and 2.5 times the legal limit for hexavalent chromium. Town of Niagara homeowners Carolyn Johnson and Jackie Linkowski received letters in March referencing the Manhattan Project, then learned their properties had radiation readings that maxed out a DEC instrument at over a million counts per minute.

Dean Baker drops a number that reframes the whole minimum wage debate: had the federal floor tracked productivity growth the way it did from 1937 to 1968, it would exceed $26 an hour today rather than sitting at $7.25 since the late 1960s. The economist from the Center for Economic and Policy Research traces union decline to a specific policy decision — the 1947 Taft-Hartley Act — and points to Canada, where roughly a third of workers remain unionized and first contracts go to mandatory arbitration, as proof that American labor's collapse reflects choices, not worker preference. DC Fiscal Policy Institute data associate Connor Zielinski puts numbers to Washington's affordability crisis: $73,000 a year for a single adult on modest estimates, $170,000 for one adult with two children, and a Black household median of $62,000 against a white household median of $174,000.

Those figures sit beside what Theater Washington president Amy Austin previews for Theater Week, September 24 through October 11. The lineup includes a Wizard of Oz retelling set on an immigrant journey from El Salvador, a Step Afrika! piece commissioned for the country's 250th anniversary, and a Roundhouse Theatre and Olney Theatre co-production of August Wilson's *Ma Rainey's Black Bottom*. David Rabin hosts *Community Watch and Comment*.

Demolition debris from the White House East Wing — containing arsenic — was dumped into East Potomac Golf Links at Hains Point without testing for two weeks, then seeded over with grass. That disclosure comes from Rebecca Miller of the DC Preservation League, one of several voices in David Rabin's Community Watch and Comment challenging Trump's plan to convert the century-old public course into a championship-level facility. Golfer Alex Dixon, cyclist Nailet Broadnax, and Washington Area Bicyclists Association emeritus member Peter Harnick detail how the proposal would reshape Ohio Drive for everyone using it. Green Party House candidate Sam Husseini describes standing up at a National Press Club event to challenge Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, being walked out by security, and receiving a lifetime ban from the club.

Post-Classical Ensemble music director Ángel Ordóñez, curator Murray Horwitz, and jazz director Chuck Redd preview their September 23rd concert at the Shakespeare Theatre. It opens with Gershwin's "I Got Rhythm" and draws on the Coltrane-Ellington album for an arrangement of Ellington's "In a Sentimental Mood.

Richard Pryor walked into Lorton prison, saw a gymnasium packed with roughly 1,000 incarcerated men, and wept. Roach Brown, host of *Crossroads Today*, was there, and he tells it live from Ben's Chili Bowl on this unscheduled open-phone hour, hosted by David Rabin after both booked guests canceled. Pryor went on to arrange for Brown's prison drama group, the Inner Voices, to perform at the Apollo Theater, Sing Sing, and Walpole State Prison.

The open phone draws callers who press Brown on returning-citizen voting rights in D.C. and Maryland, including the history of Public Law 179, introduced by Arrington Dixon in 1979 or 1980, and a Pennsylvania case where a woman received 53 years under felony murder rules for acting as a lookout. Brown also addresses the unmarked graves found at the Cheltenham boys' school in Maryland and shares the story of a man who had not encountered an automatic-flush toilet or a cellphone in 50 years.

On this episode of *Community Watch and Comment*, host David Rabin speaks with former Biden administration Head Start director Khari Garvin and National Head Start Association Deputy Director Tommy Sheridan about the Trump administration's proposed rewrite of Head Start's program performance standards — a document that would shrink from 122 pages to roughly a dozen. Garvin walks through specific rollbacks in the proposal: raising infant-to-teacher ratios from 1-to-4 to as high as 1-to-11 in some states, making health and dental screenings optional, removing pay parity requirements for teachers, and mandating English-only instruction — changes he calls "a carcass" of the original program, while Sheridan notes the public comment period runs until October 6th. The second half features Institute for Policy Studies Program Director Lindsay Kashgarian, whose organization's blueprint *Forging a Democracy That Works for All* documents that the United States' 977 billionaires now hold over $9 trillion in wealth — a 32% increase in a single year — and proposes an annual federal wealth tax on fortunes above $50 million, taxing investment income at least at the same rate as wages, and cutting the Pentagon budget in half, which Kashgarian says would, in year one alone, erase all medical debt and all private student loan debt in the country.

On the morning of September 21, 1976, a car bomb killed Orlando Letelier and Ronni Moffitt at Sheridan Circle on Embassy Row — less than two miles from the White House. Moffitt was 25, an Institute for Policy Studies staffer who had opened a music center in a low-income Washington neighborhood where people could borrow instruments for free. David Rabin, who presents the program as Host Dave Raven, speaks with IPS Global Economy Project Director Sarah Anderson about three former Chilean secret police agents sentenced to 15 years in prison for Moffitt's murder, nearly 50 years after the assassination, and about American operative Michael Townley — who taped the bomb under the car — still living in U.S. witness protection. Elliot Nagan of the Substack publication Money Trail traces Trump's "communists are coming" rhetoric back through Roy Cohn and the McCarthy era. Organizer Burton Bollag describes a weekly Saturday demonstration outside D.C.'s Holocaust Museum, where he and a small group hand out leaflets connecting the museum's historical mission to what the Committee to Protect Journalists has called the deadliest and most deliberate effort to kill journalists it has ever documented.

Taylor Fraser McCollum's family homes sit less than a mile from the site of a proposed $5 billion, 820-megawatt data center campus in Landover. She launched a Change.org petition against it; after the Party for Socialism and Liberation promoted it on Instagram, signatures reached 25,000. David Rabin speaks with McCollum, who credits that pressure with securing Prince George's County's two-year moratorium and now argues for an outright ban on hyperscale data centers, warning that even closed-loop cooling systems discharge wastewater containing biocides, heavy metals, and corrosion inhibitors into the Potomac River — ranked the most endangered river in the United States. Steve Shapiro of Praxis Energy, who has testified before the Montgomery County Council, offers a different path: host communities issue requests for information that set enforceable terms on energy sourcing, property values, and noise before any developer enters negotiations. He points to a Google pilot in New Jersey that installs solar and battery equipment directly in residents' homes as one possible template.

Roach Brown says Dr. Frances Cress Welsing saved him from the electric chair — a fact, he notes, that most people who know her work have never heard. Brown did 14 years in prison and started his radio career at Lorton Reformatory with Petey Greene in 1973. He hosts this edition of *Crossroads Today* live from Ben's Chili Bowl, with David Rabin presenting.

His guest, Jay Jefferson, spent nine years as a correctional officer at Lorton from 1989 to 1998 and has written *Lorton Penitentiary: Rules Are Meant to Be Broken*. Jefferson describes arranging with a trusted inmate to protect a frightened fellow officer on his days off, and having a prisoner named Buddy Love back him in a confrontation over a bag of cigarettes — the same man he later recruited to speak to at-risk youth after Jefferson moved to the Metropolitan Police Department. Jefferson also notes that Welsing testified as the first Black psychiatrist at St. Elizabeths Hospital.

Abby Rozner found her 36 interview subjects — elders using psilocybin and other psychedelics to make peace with mortality, heal trauma, and build community — simply by attending integration circles run by local psychedelic societies. Her book, *Psychedelics and the Counterculture of Aging*, grew from those conversations. She tells host David Rabin how ibogaine, a sacred medicine from the Bwiti people of Gabon, traveled a chain from Rick Perry to Joe Rogan to Trump himself, and raises the question of who profits when indigenous intellectual property enters pharmaceutical development. The second half moves to Mosaic Theater's 2025-26 season, where Artistic Director Reginald Douglas walks through three productions. Among them: *Somewhere Over the Border*, playwright Bryan Quijada's retelling of his Salvadoran mother's immigration story as *The Wizard of Oz*, set to cumbia, mariachi, hip-hop, and rock, and the world premiere of *7th Street Echo*, a go-go music play set in Congress Heights, developed with the Go-Go Museum in Anacostia.

people.name: Ayize Sabater
bio: Ayize Sabater is a veteran educational organizer, researcher, and author who has spent over three decades championing community-centered learning and social justice. On WPFW, he serves as the lead host and programmer for #UMustLearn, a liberatory educational program designed to inform, inspire, and ignite the local community into action. Since 2020, he has used this platform to interrogate the educational experience through the lens of equity and school reform, providing a voice for those often overlooked by mainstream media.

Ayize's connection to the station began in his mid-20s, when he supported the WPFW community as both a listener and a local business owner. During that time, his restaurant, Delights of the Garden, became a staple of station life by providing vegetarian food donations to sustain volunteers during pledge drives. His journey from a business supporter to an on-air personality was driven by his firm belief that public media is essential for allowing regular citizens to voice their concerns and advocate for their own advancement.

A globally recognized expert in his field, Ayize is widely known as the "#GodFather of Black Montessori work." His lifelong commitment to educational excellence was notably recognized by former First Lady Michelle Obama for his work with M.O.M.I.E's TLC. His research and community organizing efforts have been featured in major national publications, including the New York Times and Black Enterprise.

Beyond the airwaves, Ayize is a man of deep reflection and resilience who finds inspiration in reading, positive company, and conscious Hip-Hop. He brings a profound sense of empathy to his work, shaped by his personal journey navigating significant life hardships, including the loss of his namesake son to a mental health crisis. Guided by his mantra to "Advance the Culture," Ayize remains dedicated to using the power of the microphone to educate, empower, and strengthen the community he serves.

eps.desc: In 1957, Louis Armstrong publicly condemned the federal government's failure to protect the Little Rock Nine and refused a State Department tour in protest — and host Daman Harris opens this episode of *You Must Learn* by connecting that refusal to the 1963 bombing of the 16th Street Baptist Church, which killed four Black girls. New co-host Amy Watkins, a children's author, wrote a character with albinism after a student in her classroom had the condition. Tara Liebert of Free Minds Book Club — founded at the dying request of Glenn McGinnis, executed in 2000 at age 17 after writing from death row to ask for a book club for incarcerated youth — walks through the organization's Read for Youth Justice reading list, including its section on children with incarcerated parents. Richard Rogers, a principal leadership coach three weeks into his role at Prince George's County Public Schools, reflects on 33 years in education and being repeatedly assigned to high-need schools as a Black man on the assumption he could "wave a magic wand," while being denied the option of leading more affluent ones.

A 65-year-old Black man can be biologically closer to 68 — not by calendar, but by what Dr. Tali Elliott called "sustained high-intensity trauma" and a "weathering effect" that accumulates over a lifetime. Dr. Jeffrey Johnson, coordinator of Black Men's Health at the African American Health Program, explained this to host Dr. Daryl Howard, alongside the stark gap: average life expectancy of 70.8 years for Black men versus 75.8 for white men. Johnson traced the Tuskegee Experiment's lasting grip on medical mistrust, then described his program's strategy of taking health screenings into barbershops, salons, and basketball courts, with a free Community Ambassador Training set for Saturday, 9 a.m. to noon.

That work of meeting people where they are finds a parallel in the history Kim Bishop and Troy Bishop bring to the program. They tell the story of Good Hope Union UMC in Colesville, Montgomery County — founded in 1870 by three freed Black farmers, John Powell, Tom Stewart, and Sam Jones, who bought the land from Sarah Watts. The congregation has counted the first ordained African American female pastor in the Baltimore-Washington Conference of the United Methodist Church and a Negro Leagues pitcher who played with the Newark Eagles, Birmingham Black Barons, and Atlanta Black Crackers. The Bishops describe plans to restore the 1913 sanctuary, ring its bell again, and host a free community health bazaar on September 19th.

Vaughn Bennett, a DC firefighter turned chess instructor, says the DC Chess League excluded Black DC residents from tournaments, scholarships, and leadership for nearly 80 years — a history the US Chess Federation documented in a 2022 report. Bennett has taught more than 7,000 children across 25 years. Baba Oso, a founding member of Kankuran West African Dance and Music Company, traces the banning of the drum under slavery to its role as a communication and healing tool, and previews the group's 43rd-anniversary performance at Crampton Auditorium at Howard University. Natani Victoria Lim of Embracing Equity, an Albuquerque-based nonprofit, describes its virtual workshops on building cultures of belonging in schools and a debate over whether to strip equity-related language from its website under current political pressure — a debate the team resolved by keeping the name and the mission intact. This episode of *#YouMustLearn* airs Thursday, September 3, 2026.

Toussaint L'Ouverture was lured to a meeting under a false promise of safety, captured, and left to die — and a lieutenant "a little over 20" finished the revolution and declared Haitian independence in 1804. Dr. Daryl Howard opens *#YouMustLearn* with that account before welcoming Baba Ayize and Dr. Azoma Miller, a professor of African American Studies at Ohio University, to discuss a Black August webinar they are co-hosting through the Asen of Kemet, an African-centered fraternity founded at Morehouse as an alternative to the Divine Nine. The two argue that George Jackson, Assata Shakur, and Fred Hampton are largely absent from mainstream education. Ongoing efforts to remove exhibits about George Washington enslaving Africans at his Philadelphia house, they contend, make erasure active, not passive.

That conversation about what gets left out gives way to a look at what Words, Beats & Life is building on the ground. Mwiza Munthali, executive director of the nearly 25-year-old hip-hop nonprofit, describes their upcoming Game Day — a free intergenerational event built around chess, checkers, dominoes, Uno, spades, mahjong, and video games. This summer was the first since 2020 when young people in their programs told staff they had made friends with kids from other neighborhoods they had never met.

Andre Kearns can trace his family to Emmanuel and Joan Cumbo — captives from the Kingdom of Ndongo in present-day Angola who arrived at Port Comfort around 1628 — and to his third great-grandfather William B. Harvell, sold as a child named Buck in an 1832 bill of sale. After emancipation, Harvell became a landowner, founded a church, and established a school that launched five generations of HBCU attendance in Kearns's family, with a sixth generation now at Howard. Kearns, a Washington D.C. native, genealogist, and author, sits down with the #YouMustLearn program on WPFW to tell that story.

The episode also turns to the DiverseCITY Fund's fall grant cycle, open to Black and brown-led organizations with budgets under $50,999 that do organizing, advocacy, or healing justice work in D.C. Board member Nkechi Feaster — who first encountered the fund while living in a family shelter at D.C. General — explains how its community grantmaking model deliberately removes the barriers that typically block impacted residents from both funding decisions and funding itself. Rounding out the hour, holistic health practitioner and Black Love Day founder Mama Ayo Handy Kendi previews WPFW's 5th annual 5K walk/run on September 12th at Bladensburg Waterfront Park, describing new additions that include walking meditation and strength training.

Cliff, co-founder of Blue Montessori on Marion Barry Avenue in Anacostia, teaches 3-to-6-year-olds using go-go drumming and HBCU-style marching. He argues that Montessori's emphasis on self-direction maps directly onto the demands of college and the workplace. His tuition-free school is in its third year.

Baba Ayize's #YouMustLearn turns next to film director Ime Atuk, whose film *Outdoor School* centers on a 12-year-old boy in 1994 Portland, Oregon living under a tree with his mother and sister while guarding a pair of neon Deion Sanders patent leather Nike shoes. After audiences at screenings were repeatedly affected by the film's treatment of domestic violence, Atuk began distributing a resource guide on the subject. He also recounts meeting a 12-year-old boy outside a theater in Ashland, Oregon whose family turned out to be in a situation mirroring the film's story. *Outdoor School* screens August 15th at the George Washington University Student Center as part of the ADIFF DC festival.

Curtis Valentine's great-grandfather co-founded a Rosenwald School; his book *Real Men Teach* traces that lineage back to John Chavis, a free Black man who taught white students in the early 1800s whose student went on to become a U.S. Senator from North Carolina. Valentine, founding president of the Male Educator Network and Policy Institute, joins host Daman Harris on *You Must Learn* at WPFW, with testimony from former students of Black male educators including U.S. Senator Raphael Warnock and Governor Deval Patrick, and a discussion of figures such as Charles Ogletree. 

Baba Clifton of Mommy's TLC announces a pre-celebration at 2616 Georgia Avenue Northwest on August 1st, marking 25 years and over 16,000 children served through the out-of-school-time program. Dr. Sekou Africa of Bowie State University describes building a pipeline for Black male educators from 8th grade through master's degree level, and explains how symptoms he mistook for a stroke and a heart attack shaped his new initiative, the Black Male Educator Classroom.

people.name: Candy Shannon
bio: Candy Shannon is a veteran media professional and educator who has been a prominent voice in D.C. radio for over four decades. A native of Detroit, she began her local career in 1980 when she was recruited as the first full-time female personality at 93.9 WKYS-FM. She officially joined the WPFW family in 1998 at the invitation of then-Program Director Lou Hankins.

Throughout her distinguished career in the nation's capital, Candy has worn many hats, including narrating books for the Library of Congress, hosting a late-night video show on WUSA-Channel 9, and working in news at Voice of America and satellite radio with WorldSpace. She also served as the Host and Program Director for WDCU (Jazz 90) during its final five years of operation. Beyond her work in the booth, she is a retired educator who served as an adjunct professor and director at Howard University's Cathy Hughes School of Communications.

Today, Candy produces and hosts The Friday Morning Brew, where she celebrates the rich history and contemporary sounds of Jazz. She views the music as more than just entertainment; it is the essential soundtrack of Black life, rooted in African heritage and born out of a legacy of survival and creativity. Through her program, she aims to lift the spirits of her listeners and provide a platform that honors the stories of the musicians who keep this vital art form alive.

eps.desc:
Rusty Hassan was 17 when he told his parents he was sleeping at a friend's house, climbed into a 1954 Studebaker, and drove from Greenwich, Connecticut to Newport, Rhode Island to hear John Coltrane at the 1963 festival — staying put even as a friend tugged his sleeve because they had summer jobs to get back to. Candy Shannon's two-hour centennial program collects firsthand accounts from Washington-area musicians, each naming a favorite Coltrane recording and explaining why.

Bassist Michael Bowie and saxophonist Antonio Parker both chose "Resolution" from *A Love Supreme*. Bowie notes the track was nearly cut from the album, and that Coltrane shifted its key from B-flat to E-flat after playing it live at Pep's, a Philadelphia club. Judy Corey, curator of the Felix E. Grant Jazz Archives at UDC, selects "Alabama" and ties it directly to the 1963 Birmingham church bombing that killed four girls. Bassist Ralph Armstrong recalls that Stevie Wonder requested "Giant Steps" every time they played together.

I may look like a nice Jewish girl from New Jersey, but inside I'm a 50-year-old heavyset Black man with a big thumb, like Wes Montgomery." That's Emily Remler, speaking to *People* magazine, and she is the subject of Candy Shannon's 6 o'clock birthday-artist segment on "Friday Morning Brew." Remler died of a heart attack on tour in Australia at 32, having moved from Berklee College of Music through New Orleans blues and jazz clubs to a 1985 *DownBeat* Guitarist of the Year award. Shannon plays tracks from *East to Wes* and from Remler's final recording, *This Is Me*.

From there, commentator Skylar Borton traces today's corporate political dominance to the August 1971 Powell Memo — eight pages drafted by Richmond attorney Lewis Powell for the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, mapping a long-game strategy to reshape lobbying, the judiciary, media, and education. That Lewis Powell had previously argued on behalf of Philip Morris that smoking did not cause cancer before Nixon appointed him to the Supreme Court.

Commentator Skyler Borton covers the Treasury Department's $12.5 billion bond buyback amid foreign sell-offs and a First Circuit ruling blocking the administration's mail-in voting plan. Also in Borton's segment: Houthi control of the port of Mokka near the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait, and an Ohio resident's case that AI data center development is a speculative bubble requiring municipalities to demand upfront capital bonds before granting tax and zoning concessions. Music includes tracks from Charles Tolliver's remastered 1968 debut *Right Now and Then* — with Herbie Hancock, Ron Carter, and Gary Bartz — plus selections from Dee Dee Bridgewater's Horace Silver tribute and Cindy Blackman's *Someday*.

people.name: Andrea Thompson
bio: Andrea Thompson first found WPFW as a college student in the 1990s, listening without yet supporting the station. In 2004, at 31, she was recruited and trained into the Sophie's Parlor Women's Radio Collective by Marietta Ulacia, who was then also hosting a weeknight Latin Flavor program. She has been hooked ever since.

Andrea is an advocate for people telling their own stories, and the chance to do that at scale for women from all over the world is what keeps her in the chair. Her mantra is that everyone deserves to tell their own story, whether through their voice or through their music.

Two broadcasts stand out in her memory. While living in China between 2007 and 2008, she used Skype to call into the studio and co-produce two shows with guests in Washington, years before the pandemic made remote broadcasting routine. Colleagues at the station were amazed it worked. The other was a Saturday in the mid-2000s when Sophie's Parlor took over the station for several hours of International Women's Day programming featuring local women artists across every genre.

Sophie's Parlor is a show by women, about women, for everyone. It is the oldest continuously running women's music radio collective in the United States and has been on WPFW since 1977, carrying a music and public affairs format.

eps.desc:
A state official told Tennessee State University that funds would flow only after Glenda Glover was gone — what she calls "hush money." Glover, former TSU president and author of *How Dare You*, walks host Reverend Mark Thompson through a state-commissioned report finding that Tennessee owed TSU between $147 million and $544 million in underfunded land-grant money dating to 1958 under the 1890 Morrill Act. When $250 million was finally appropriated, restrictions confined TSU to spending roughly $18–19 million of it. The University of Tennessee faced no comparable conditions. Going public with the shortfall triggered the replacement of TSU's Board of Trustees and Glover's own departure.

The conversation moves from that reckoning to what Glover has done since. Through her organization Fair Funding (fairfunding.org), she continues pressing the issue. As Alpha Kappa Alpha president, she placed $100,000 endowments at every HBCU. And the underfunding at TSU is not singular: a federal finding determined that TSU, North Carolina A&T, and FAMU are each owed roughly $2 billion.

Helen — "your Diva of Today" — opened her two-hour *Sophie's Parlor* by anchoring the word "move" to four movements: Command, Body, March, and Arrival. Nina Simone's "Mississippi Goddam" landed mid-program with Helen's note that it "makes 100% sense right now too." The musical arc stretched from Cassandra Wilson's "You Gotta Move" and Odetta's Spiritual Trilogy through Billie Holiday, Sarah Vaughan, Esperanza Spalding, and Diane Reeves. News breaks covered a federal judge blocking Trump's attempt to rename the Kennedy Center, the Federal Reserve's first interest rate increase in more than three years, and a class-action lawsuit against the NIH over 235 keywords used to cancel scientific grants.

Errin Haines attended the Houston memorial for Lorenzo Salgado-Araujo and sat down with Latasha Brown — a daughter of Selma — to talk about the Supreme Court's voting rights decision, all as part of season one of her video series *Long Play*. Haines, president of the National Association of Black Journalists, editor-at-large and co-founder of The 19th, tells host Reverend Mark Thompson how she and her co-hosts reported directly from Georgia, North Carolina, South Carolina, Texas, Mississippi, and Tennessee. She breaks down the Georgia governor's race between Keisha Lance Bottoms and billionaire Rick Jackson, flags that 600,000 Black women have been forced out of the workforce, and notes seven Black women running statewide on the Georgia ballot this cycle.

Those threads carry into the open phones, where callers weigh in on why some Latino and Black voters support candidates whose policies target their own communities, the case for multi-party democracy, and whether election results will be certified.

Eighty-four percent of maternal deaths in Washington, D.C. are Black women, and the July closure of the postpartum and antepartum unit at Washington Hospital Center is making things worse. A community forum on the issue is set for September 9th at People's Church with mayor-elect Janice Lewis George. National Nurses United director Jazmyn reports that Medicare for All now has 115 House co-sponsors and 17 in the Senate — the most ever — with Senator Chris Van Hollen and Representatives April McClain Delaney and Sarah Elfreth signing on for the first time last December.

Calling in from the Greenbelt Labor Day parade, Metropolitan Washington AFL-CIO president Sam Epps reports that workers at Verbal Beginnings, a Rockville company serving people with developmental disabilities, have been on strike for seven weeks through Teamsters 639. A recent Gallup poll puts union favorability at 71% nationally, with 47 million workers who want to join one but cannot. To Heal DC host Joni Eisenberg anchors the two-hour Labor Day program.

Gabriel Prosser's plan was precise: seize the armory, kidnap the governor or James Madison, and trade them for freedom. Lawrence Hamm, chair of the People's Organization for Progress in New Jersey, walks host Joni through that 1800 Virginia rebellion and the execution of roughly 26 of its participants — pardoned posthumously by Tim Kaine centuries later. From there the two move through Black August's bloodier landmarks: the Peekskill riots of August 27 and September 4, 1949, when racist mobs and police coordinating with the Klan attacked concertgoers at Paul Robeson's concerts. Emmett Till's killers confessed in a paid *Life* magazine interview and were acquitted by an all-white jury — which is exactly why the March on Washington was scheduled for August 28th.

Hamm connects the ongoing power outage in Gary, Indiana to that city's role hosting the 1972 National Black Political Convention, and the hour closes on Hurricane Katrina's August 29, 2005 anniversary.

Senator John Tyler Morgan — a former Klansman — described Black suffrage as a load to be rid of "by burning down the barn to kill the rats." DC historian C.R. Gibbs cites Morgan's role in stripping the vote from every DC resident after the Civil War, then traces Josephine Butler's leadership of the DC Statehood Party from 1977 through the 1990s. Walter Fauntroy's statehood bill cleared the House District Committee but never reached the floor. Eleanor Holmes Norton's 1993 bill lost 277 to 153. DC Statehood Party candidate Kamau Freeman adds that Butler's organizing directly stopped a planned expressway through the Brookland neighborhood.

WPFW morning host Brother Jamil will debut a one-man play about his life at the Billie Holiday Theater in Bedford-Stuyvesant on August 29th and 30th.

A Maryland man tells *Make It Plain* host Reverend Mark Thompson he has not voted in nearly 70 years. That call opens a wide-ranging phones segment on third-party politics — the Umoja Party, the Working Families Party, the DSA — alongside a Virginia political consultant running four Northern Virginia races who argues the Democratic Party would be four separate parties if it were in Europe.

Terrence Woodbury, president of HIT Strategies, then presents findings from his organization's *State of Black Opposition and Engagement* research. Among the results: 62% of Black respondents said no one had asked them to join resistance activities, and Black approval of ICE sits at 6%. The share of Black Americans taking three or more civic actions climbed from 64% in October 2025 to 75% by April, a rise Woodbury ties partly to what he calls the "Kale decision" and escalating attacks on Black political power in the South. His polling also shows that corporations and special interests rank above Donald Trump on Black voters' list of who is most responsible for undermining democracy.

Among Black women who call themselves progressive, 54% of Gen Z also identify as Democratic Socialists — a number that stops Reverend Mark A. Thompson and Brother Minister Jamil Muhammad cold. Dr. Avis Jones-DeWeaver brings the data: the Annual Black Women's Roundtable Power of the Silent Vote Poll shows a 20-point surge in Black women's motivation to vote compared to two years earlier, and a 17-point increase since 2024 in the share identifying as strongly Democrat. Thompson and Muhammad tie the shift to federal worker layoffs, cuts to SNAP, and attacks on affirmative action, framing each as part of what they call an ongoing assault on Black women's economic security.

The broadcast falls during WPFW's summer pledge drive. Thompson also tells a story about his grandfather, director of admissions at Fisk University, where a young Marion Barry was a student before he came to Washington.

Rashad Robinson walked out of a meeting with Mark Zuckerberg and Sheryl Sandberg rather than sign an NDA — weeks after the New York Times revealed Facebook had hired a PR firm to target him and Color of Change. His new book *From Presence to Power* argues the civil rights movement ran on economic leverage and organizational infrastructure, and that social media visibility is not the same thing as power.

Dr. Wes Bellamy of the John Mercer Langston Institute at Virginia State University brings findings from nearly 10,000 engagements with Black men nationwide. Black men's unemployment hit 7.3% in April 2025, the highest among the four major Bureau of Labor Statistics racial groups. Black fourth-grade boys read at a 17% proficiency level. Bellamy also challenges the idea that the trades are a clean alternative to college, pointing to systemic barriers that block Black tradesmen from foreman roles and city contracts, keeping many earning as subcontractors. Host Reverend Mark Thompson leads the conversation on *Make It Plain*.

people.name: DJ Underdog
bio: DJ Underdog is a Washington, D.C.-based DJ, educator, designer, and community organizer whose work seamlessly connects global music, culture, and social consciousness. As the host of Black Star Radio on WPFW 89.3 FM, he takes listeners on a late-night journey through the music and voices of Africa, the Caribbean, and the wider global Black diaspora.

On his program, DJ Underdog blends carefully curated music with thoughtful storytelling and conversations about history, art, wellness, and food sovereignty. He views the airwaves as a gateway to the people and movements behind the sound, creating a space where community members can hear their cultures respected and their questions explored. For him, independent radio is a vital tool to preserve culture, challenge dominant narratives, and amplify stories that are too often overlooked by commercial media.

Beyond the station, DJ Underdog is a prominent figure in the creative community who has produced events and performed alongside world-renowned artists such as Questlove, Thundercat, Sango, and Femi Kuti. His work and insights have also been featured on platforms like OkayAfrica, AFROPUNK, and MoCADA. Despite navigating personal hardships and health challenges, he remains deeply committed to using music and education as tools for community resilience and transformation.

Guided by the mantra "Music is the message, community is the purpose," DJ Underdog is passionate about the future of public media. He encourages the WPFW family, especially younger listeners, to stay curious and bring their own imagination and technology to the airwaves. His advice to the next generation is simple: do not allow trends or algorithms to define your identity.

eps.desc: Zaya Ross has been playing "message music" in what he calls "Babylon Central" for 25 years — and in a live phone interview with DJ Underdog, he explains how France's demand for restitution from Haiti after independence moved him to write "Sweet Haiti." Ross's DC reggae band Proverbs takes its name from a commitment to sharing ancestral wisdom, and the band was set to perform at the WPFW Jazz and Justice Festival in Malcolm X Park that Sunday. A caller named Naima requests Wayne Wade's "Lady," a 33-inch record she bought at a community record shop in Virginia decades ago and covered in her own artwork. DJ Underdog marks birthdays for King Sunny Ade and U-Roy, plays music from La Réunion Island at a listener's request, and includes a remembrance of Betsy Jean Farrakhan. Audrey Monet's spoken-word piece "The Water's Still Rising" also features in the hour. Black Star Radio aired Monday, September 21, 2026 at 10:00 pm on WPFW.

A voice in archival audio explains that South Africa's Black Consciousness Movement existed to make Black people "proud of themselves, proud of their color" — to counter the psychological frustration, as the speaker put it, of striving to become white under apartheid. DJ Underdog builds the episode around that foundation, moving through Ethiopian jazz, Studio One reggae, Yoruba percussion, and tracks from Tanzania including Makadem's "Muhogo wa Jengombe." He dedicates selections to Enkutatash, the Ethiopian New Year, and pauses to note that Ethiopia runs on a 13-month calendar he calls "the true calendar." Jamaican dub poet Rashadai gets a spotlight placing him in the lineage of Mutabaruka and Linton Kwesi Johnson. The episode closes with a live salon session recorded by Yardcore at Sweet V in Brooklyn, previewing a mixtape called *Reggae Aroma Volume 5*.

people.name: Amy Watkins
bio: Amy L. Watkins is a National Board Certified teacher, award-winning children's author, and dedicated literacy advocate who serves as a collective member and host for #UMustLearn on WPFW. A lifelong resident of the DMV, Amy grew up with 89.3 FM as a constant companion, always keeping a button on her car radio programmed to the station.

In her professional life, Amy is the founder of Sadie Bug Publishing LLC and has focused much of her career on supporting multilingual learners. She is passionate about mentoring aspiring authors through community events and her podcast, always seeking to create opportunities for people of all ages to learn and grow. On the airwaves, she finds joy in amplifying the voices of educators and changemakers to spark curiosity and connection. She is guided by the firm belief that everyone has a story worth telling, and every story has the power to teach.

Amy views WPFW as an essential space for thoughtful conversation and diverse perspectives that encourage critical thinking rather than quick reactions. She is particularly rewarded when listeners are inspired by her interviews to pick up a new book or see a community issue from a fresh perspective. Her advice to the WPFW community, especially younger listeners, is to stay curious, ask deep questions, and never underestimate the power of their own stories.

eps.desc: A veteran in a wheelchair looked at a three-legged hound named Tripod and said, "the two of us got a similar injury, we're both tripods." That moment at the Armed Forces Retirement Home in Washington, D.C., launched veterinarian Dr. Tanis Johnson into decades of certifying therapy animals — which she recounts here with host Dr. Theodore Watkins on *To Your Health*. Resident nutritionist Dr. Ruby Lathan tackles fall eating: vegan cheese made from cashews or from potatoes and carrots, and why phytoestrogens in soy are protective, not harmful — what she calls "propaganda" to the contrary. Reiki practitioner Maisie Coleman describes using Reiki and reflexology to carry her own dog through a year of kidney failure, and announces the 12th Annual Reiki Animal Blessing, a free outdoor event on October 3rd at 1225 R Street NW.

In 1957, Louis Armstrong publicly condemned the federal government's failure to protect the Little Rock Nine and refused a State Department tour in protest — and host Daman Harris opens this episode of *You Must Learn* by connecting that refusal to the 1963 bombing of the 16th Street Baptist Church, which killed four Black girls. New co-host Amy Watkins, a children's author, wrote a character with albinism after a student in her classroom had the condition. Tara Liebert of Free Minds Book Club — founded at the dying request of Glenn McGinnis, executed in 2000 at age 17 after writing from death row to ask for a book club for incarcerated youth — walks through the organization's Read for Youth Justice reading list, including its section on children with incarcerated parents. Richard Rogers, a principal leadership coach three weeks into his role at Prince George's County Public Schools, reflects on 33 years in education and being repeatedly assigned to high-need schools as a Black man on the assumption he could "wave a magic wand," while being denied the option of leading more affluent ones.

A grain of sugar-sized piece of lead can permanently strip a child of one IQ point. Al Hawkins, president and CEO of Millman Systems, explains exactly how that happens on this edition of **To Your Health**: the body can't tell lead from calcium, so lead stored in a mother's bones can leach into her bloodstream during pregnancy and cross the placenta. Host Dr. Theodore Watkins and producer Frank Smith press Hawkins on the broader consequences. Studies tie lead exposure to aggressive behavior, criminal behavior, and high school dropout rates, with lower-income neighborhoods bearing the heaviest burden. Hawkins also outlines a planned phytoremediation pilot in West Baltimore — modeled on Chernobyl cleanup methods — using plants with an expanded root zone to pull heavy metals from vacant-lot soil, then burning the harvest in a closed-loop incinerator to keep contaminants out of the Patapsco River and Chesapeake Bay.

The hour closes closer to home. A representative recruits African American women ages 40 to 75 for the Prime Time Sister Circle program — free, 12 weeks, conducted virtually, and funded in part by Montgomery County government — covering hypertension, stress, nutrition, and fitness.

A 65-year-old Black man can be biologically closer to 68 — not by calendar, but by what Dr. Tali Elliott called "sustained high-intensity trauma" and a "weathering effect" that accumulates over a lifetime. Dr. Jeffrey Johnson, coordinator of Black Men's Health at the African American Health Program, explained this to host Dr. Daryl Howard, alongside the stark gap: average life expectancy of 70.8 years for Black men versus 75.8 for white men. Johnson traced the Tuskegee Experiment's lasting grip on medical mistrust, then described his program's strategy of taking health screenings into barbershops, salons, and basketball courts, with a free Community Ambassador Training set for Saturday, 9 a.m. to noon.

That work of meeting people where they are finds a parallel in the history Kim Bishop and Troy Bishop bring to the program. They tell the story of Good Hope Union UMC in Colesville, Montgomery County — founded in 1870 by three freed Black farmers, John Powell, Tom Stewart, and Sam Jones, who bought the land from Sarah Watts. The congregation has counted the first ordained African American female pastor in the Baltimore-Washington Conference of the United Methodist Church and a Negro Leagues pitcher who played with the Newark Eagles, Birmingham Black Barons, and Atlanta Black Crackers. The Bishops describe plans to restore the 1913 sanctuary, ring its bell again, and host a free community health bazaar on September 19th.

Lifeguarding is probably 85% prevention," says a 59-year Asbury Park lifeguard explaining why drownings on guarded beaches are near zero. That claim opens an hour drawn from six podcasts across the Labor Radio Podcast Network. Two United Steelworkers members who work 2,150 feet underground at the Waste Isolation Pilot Plant in New Mexico — the only facility in the world that disposes of nuclear waste underground — describe it as "its own little city" with ambulances, electricians, and fire protection. A Calgary freelance journalist traces her turning point to an all-nighter at an architecture firm when a boss arrived at 3 a.m. demanding drawing changes, realizing then "this is why workers unionize."

Australian construction workers from the Concrete Gang react to police raiding union officials' homes, cops walking through asking "how did you afford this?" From there the hour turns to Colorado labor history: the 1927 Columbine Mine Massacre, the IWW's role in what historians call the most successful strike in Colorado history, and Big Bill Haywood's connection to the founding of the IWW. Hosted by Chris Garlock with Patrick Dixon and Harold Phillips.

Vaughn Bennett, a DC firefighter turned chess instructor, says the DC Chess League excluded Black DC residents from tournaments, scholarships, and leadership for nearly 80 years — a history the US Chess Federation documented in a 2022 report. Bennett has taught more than 7,000 children across 25 years. Baba Oso, a founding member of Kankuran West African Dance and Music Company, traces the banning of the drum under slavery to its role as a communication and healing tool, and previews the group's 43rd-anniversary performance at Crampton Auditorium at Howard University. Natani Victoria Lim of Embracing Equity, an Albuquerque-based nonprofit, describes its virtual workshops on building cultures of belonging in schools and a debate over whether to strip equity-related language from its website under current political pressure — a debate the team resolved by keeping the name and the mission intact. This episode of *#YouMustLearn* airs Thursday, September 3, 2026.

Bob Dole took to the Senate floor and threatened NPR's funding — and according to Noelle Hanrahan, founder of Prison Radio, that threat is the direct reason prisons banned recording equipment. Hanrahan tells host Katea Stitt how Democracy Now dropped from 26 stations to 13 after it began airing commentaries by Mumia Abu-Jamal.

Abu-Jamal himself then calls in from SCI Mahanoy. His PhD dissertation takes up the transformation between the man who wrote *Black Skin, White Masks* and the man who wrote *The Wretched of the Earth* — two versions of Frantz Fanon — and from there he moves to fear as a tool of empire, the ICE killing of Alex Preddy in Minneapolis, and AI as a mechanism for concentrating wealth among the super-rich. The episode is part of WPFW's Black August special, broadcast Monday, August 31, 2026.

Toussaint L'Ouverture was lured to a meeting under a false promise of safety, captured, and left to die — and a lieutenant "a little over 20" finished the revolution and declared Haitian independence in 1804. Dr. Daryl Howard opens *#YouMustLearn* with that account before welcoming Baba Ayize and Dr. Azoma Miller, a professor of African American Studies at Ohio University, to discuss a Black August webinar they are co-hosting through the Asen of Kemet, an African-centered fraternity founded at Morehouse as an alternative to the Divine Nine. The two argue that George Jackson, Assata Shakur, and Fred Hampton are largely absent from mainstream education. Ongoing efforts to remove exhibits about George Washington enslaving Africans at his Philadelphia house, they contend, make erasure active, not passive.

That conversation about what gets left out gives way to a look at what Words, Beats & Life is building on the ground. Mwiza Munthali, executive director of the nearly 25-year-old hip-hop nonprofit, describes their upcoming Game Day — a free intergenerational event built around chess, checkers, dominoes, Uno, spades, mahjong, and video games. This summer was the first since 2020 when young people in their programs told staff they had made friends with kids from other neighborhoods they had never met.

Dr. Theodore Watkins, a surgeon-turned-holistic-medicine practitioner, devotes this episode of *To Your Health* to the physiology of walking, drawing on his own "Walk for Life" program he ran with residents of Harvard Towers — a high-rise near 16th and Harvard — where elderly patients who had rarely left their apartments eventually walked to the National Zoo. Watkins explains in clinical detail how the calf muscles (the soleus and gastrocnemius) act as a mechanical sump pump returning blood to the heart, how walking produces nitric oxide that relaxes arterial walls, and how a glucose transporter called GLUT4 clears blood sugar without insulin — relevant, he argues, to reversing rather than merely managing diabetes and early-stage Alzheimer's. Callers raise questions about neuropathy, hypoglycemia, and a brain parasite linked to a public official, and Watkins cites research suggesting that breast, colorectal, and prostate cancer survivors who walk regularly can see a 30 to 40 percent reduction in cancer-specific and all-cause mortality.

Andre Kearns can trace his family to Emmanuel and Joan Cumbo — captives from the Kingdom of Ndongo in present-day Angola who arrived at Port Comfort around 1628 — and to his third great-grandfather William B. Harvell, sold as a child named Buck in an 1832 bill of sale. After emancipation, Harvell became a landowner, founded a church, and established a school that launched five generations of HBCU attendance in Kearns's family, with a sixth generation now at Howard. Kearns, a Washington D.C. native, genealogist, and author, sits down with the #YouMustLearn program on WPFW to tell that story.

The episode also turns to the DiverseCITY Fund's fall grant cycle, open to Black and brown-led organizations with budgets under $50,999 that do organizing, advocacy, or healing justice work in D.C. Board member Nkechi Feaster — who first encountered the fund while living in a family shelter at D.C. General — explains how its community grantmaking model deliberately removes the barriers that typically block impacted residents from both funding decisions and funding itself. Rounding out the hour, holistic health practitioner and Black Love Day founder Mama Ayo Handy Kendi previews WPFW's 5th annual 5K walk/run on September 12th at Bladensburg Waterfront Park, describing new additions that include walking meditation and strength training.

Richard Van Dyke walked 4.5 to 5 miles a day, steamed unseasoned asparagus and kale, and brought his hemoglobin A1c from 6.5 down to 5.5 — then came off diabetes medication entirely. Attorney Patricia Grady grew organic vegetables across four garden plots at her church, drank 64 ounces of alkaline water daily, and watched her blood pressure drop from readings as high as 180–190 to 118/77. Host Dr. Theodore Watkins, now approaching 50 years since his medical school portrait went up on the wall, argues that lifestyle intervention was once the first line of treatment in medical textbooks before it largely disappeared from practice. On *To Your Health*, he interviews both patients about the diet changes, cleansing program, and daily check-ins that drove those results.

Van Dyke and Grady walk through the specifics of what the shift looked like for each of them.

Dr. Theodore Watkins, host of *To Your Health*, once quit sugar and watched his chronic headaches disappear — then traced the cause back to his Saturday-night strawberry milkshake habit. From that starting point he explains how hyper-palatable foods trigger the brain's dopamine and endorphin systems the same way opiates do, with roughly 20% of the U.S. population affected and women addicted at nearly twice the rate of men. Treatment approaches include elimination diets, cognitive behavioral therapy, and fasting.

Co-host Frank Smith brings his own measure of what those changes can mean: he is now 13 years past a 2013 cancer diagnosis that gave him a six-percent survival chance, a margin he attributes to lifestyle change. Watkins widens the lens further, connecting Black Americans' kidney failure rate — four times that of white Americans — to diet-related hypertension and diabetes rather than genetics alone.

Cliff, co-founder of Blue Montessori on Marion Barry Avenue in Anacostia, teaches 3-to-6-year-olds using go-go drumming and HBCU-style marching. He argues that Montessori's emphasis on self-direction maps directly onto the demands of college and the workplace. His tuition-free school is in its third year.

Baba Ayize's #YouMustLearn turns next to film director Ime Atuk, whose film *Outdoor School* centers on a 12-year-old boy in 1994 Portland, Oregon living under a tree with his mother and sister while guarding a pair of neon Deion Sanders patent leather Nike shoes. After audiences at screenings were repeatedly affected by the film's treatment of domestic violence, Atuk began distributing a resource guide on the subject. He also recounts meeting a 12-year-old boy outside a theater in Ashland, Oregon whose family turned out to be in a situation mirroring the film's story. *Outdoor School* screens August 15th at the George Washington University Student Center as part of the ADIFF DC festival.

A woman on nearly 20 medications told Dr. Theodore Watkins that her lifelong pork habit had done her no harm. That patient anchors the hour — **To Your Health**, Monday, August 3, 2026 — as Watkins and co-host Frank Smith dig into why people keep eating food they know is hurting them. The problem, Watkins argues, isn't ignorance. It's dopamine hijacking by ultra-processed food corporations that recruited scientists from tobacco companies, social pressure at family dinners, and what he calls "familiar toxicity feeling safer than positive change." He cites men in rural Africa being forty times less likely to develop prostate cancer than men in the United States.

The broadcast also carries a news break reporting the death of Arlene Smith, original lead singer of the Chantels and writer of their 1958 million-selling hit "Maybe.

Curtis Valentine's great-grandfather co-founded a Rosenwald School; his book *Real Men Teach* traces that lineage back to John Chavis, a free Black man who taught white students in the early 1800s whose student went on to become a U.S. Senator from North Carolina. Valentine, founding president of the Male Educator Network and Policy Institute, joins host Daman Harris on *You Must Learn* at WPFW, with testimony from former students of Black male educators including U.S. Senator Raphael Warnock and Governor Deval Patrick, and a discussion of figures such as Charles Ogletree. 

Baba Clifton of Mommy's TLC announces a pre-celebration at 2616 Georgia Avenue Northwest on August 1st, marking 25 years and over 16,000 children served through the out-of-school-time program. Dr. Sekou Africa of Bowie State University describes building a pipeline for Black male educators from 8th grade through master's degree level, and explains how symptoms he mistook for a stroke and a heart attack shaped his new initiative, the Black Male Educator Classroom.

people.name: Craig Williams
bio: Craig Williams has been a devoted part of the WPFW community since the station's very first broadcast in 1977. While he was a student in architecture school, Craig began a lifelong journey with the station as a loyal listener and member, eventually becoming a major donor and volunteer activist. After decades of support, Craig realized his childhood dream of becoming a DJ when his sister, Miyuki Williams, trained him to operate the control board in 2016.

Today, Craig hosts Morning Brew — Classic Jazz Edition, where he guides listeners through a curated selection of straight-ahead jazz, bebop, and brand-new releases. A self-proclaimed jazz nerd, he loves to experiment by blending blues, gospel, and even rock and roll into his sets to create a unique, curated experience for his audience. Craig believes deeply in the power of curated radio over computer algorithms, aiming to provide programming that enlightens the mind and strengthens the soul.

Beyond the airwaves, Craig is a mostly-retired architect with a passion for urban photography, dog rescue, and world travel. When he isn't attending live jazz performances, he is often in his kitchen, cooking gourmet meals without recipes using fresh ingredients from his own backyard garden.

eps.desc: From a concert stage in Paris to the frenzied late-night drive of Graz and Comblain-la-Tour, Belgium, Craig Williams plays John Coltrane's European recordings in strict chronological order so the evolution speaks for itself. The two-hour block draws from *So Many Things: The European Tour 1961* on Acrobat and archival recordings from Copenhagen, Stockholm, and Baden-Baden, tracing the rotating lineups of Eric Dolphy, McCoy Tyner, Jimmy Garrison, and Elvin Jones as the group moves from melodic early sets toward something harder and more relentless. Williams notes that Coltrane was born in Hamlet, North Carolina, and points to young Chicago tenor player Isaiah Collier as someone carrying that tradition forward. The program aired as part of a station-wide day of Coltrane centennial programming running from morning to midnight on September 23, 2026.

Mumia Abu-Jamal told Dave Zirin "they're at war against history because their agenda demands ignorance" — and that line sits at the center of Zirin's new biography *The People's Historian: The Outsized Life of Howard Zinn*, which he discusses with host Miyuki Williams on *A Sunday Kind of Love*. Zirin, sports editor of *The Nation* and WPFW co-host, traces how Zinn's method of telling history from the bottom up shaped his own sportswriting. Ziah Ayubu of Proverbs Reggae Band — formed in D.C. after he relocated from New York in 2000 — previews the band's set at the WPFW Jazz and Justice Festival at Meridian Hill Malcolm X Park. Filmmakers Merawi Gerima and Jordan Strudwick discuss the festival's film program, including Gerima's 2020 gentrification drama *Residue*, shot near North Capitol and Florida Avenue largely with non-actor D.C. residents, alongside the new Sun Ra documentary *Do the Impossible*. Music across the hour draws from Donald Byrd's *A New Perspective*, a Brandon Woody track from *For the Love of It All*, Nina Simone, Ray Charles, and John Coltrane, with Williams marking Coltrane's 100th birthday and an all-day WPFW tribute airing the following Wednesday.

Craig Williams built a 75-minute water-themed set around Pharoah Sanders playing Coltrane's "After the Rain," then moved through Gregory Porter, Charlie Haden and Hank Jones on "Wade in the Water," and three back-to-back versions of "Bridge Over Troubled Waters" — Aretha Franklin with King Curtis on reeds and Billy Preston on organ, Roberta Flack, and Eva Cassidy recorded live at Blues Alley. Faith and Harmony closed that stretch.

From there the show turned to a live 1987 Leon Thomas and Gary Bartz performance from Baltimore's long-gone Ethel's, followed by three versions of "The Creator Has a Master Plan": the original Pharoah Sanders recording — Sanders credited as Little Rock — and a new reading by D.C. vocalist Ekep Nkwelle on Mack Avenue. The Sullivan Fortner Trio then performed "Shaw Nuff" live at the Bim Haas in Amsterdam. Williams closed with an Alan Harris album of songs written entirely by Ike Joseph, signing off with the note that an upcoming album would be turning 50 on the 28th — reason enough, he said, to play it.

eps.desc:
Silvio Rodriguez calls it "a slow Gaza." Dr. James Counts Early, just back from Cuba, told host Faye Williams that U.S. sanctions have pushed infant mortality there from 4.4 to 9.9 per 1,000 births and that Cuba produced five COVID vaccines while the U.S. blocked needle shipments. Early was promoting that evening's forum, "Resolving the US-Provoked Crisis in Cuba: Normalizing Relations with Our Neighbor," at New York Avenue Baptist Church at 7 p.m.

Songwriter Troy Davis and Dr. Stephanie Myers of Black Women for Positive Change discuss their song "Change the Culture of Violence" and the upcoming 15th annual Month of Nonviolence in October. The episode closes with William McMurray, inventor of the RAC, explaining his Operation Rack It Up program for responsible firearm storage.

Jacari Sherman traces stepping back to the Negro Act of 1740, which banned drums in colonial South Carolina and forced enslaved and free Black people to make their bodies percussive instruments. His choreography for *The Fruits of Our Labor*, Step Afrika!'s production at Arena Stage, builds one section around Reverend C.L. Franklin's sermon "The Eagle Stirreth in Her Nest" — treating the congregation's responses as central to the movement as Franklin's own cadence. Sherman names "freedom" as the single word that unlocks the entire work. Miyuki Williams presents.

That history has a present address: Meridian Hill Malcolm X Park, where Steve Coleman of Washington Parks and People recalls 20,000 people gathering one month after Dr. King's assassination to hear Pearl Bailey perform. Producer Charvis Campbell details the full-day public affairs programming planned for WPFW's September 27th Jazz and Justice Festival at that same park. The episode closes with birthday tributes to blues pianist Charles Brown and Mel Tormé, who co-wrote "The Christmas Song" in 40 minutes on a sweltering summer day.

eps.desc:
Baltimore trumpeter Brandon Woody and Chicago tenor saxophonist Isaiah Collier turned out to be college roommates from Humboldt University. They reunited on stage at Union Stage when Collier sat in for about three tunes during Woody's late evening DC Jazz Festival set. Craig Williams caught that moment and brings it to Morning Brew Classic Jazz Edition alongside Emmett Cohen's District Pier set featuring Jeremy Pelt.

The programme also covers Etienne Charles' Creole Soul Band, Joshua Redman's quartet, and the Epris, an all-woman saxophone quartet with Lauren Sevian on baritone and Chelsea Boratz on tenor. Williams closes by previewing music from DC bassist Herman Burney and Baltimore's Chris Funn, both appearing at WPFW's upcoming benefit concert.

eps.desc:
Philip Aaron Lacy, a Howard University graduate who practiced architecture in Washington, D.C. for 40 years, tells host Faye Williams that January 6th drove him to research who actually built the U.S. Capitol. His book *They Laid the Stone* recovers the enslaved workers who constructed it between 1793 and 1864, known only by first names in slave ledgers, with no identified living descendants. One of them, Philip Reed, cast the statue that stands atop the dome. A site diagonally across from the Air and Space Museum once functioned as a slave dungeon.

That same evening, the Hirshhorn Museum hosts the premiere of *The Capital*, a film about the political battles over choosing the nation's capital, directed by Dr. Amy Anderson, daughter of former D.C. Mayor Sharon Pratt. The episode also notes a September 16th forum titled "Resolving the US-Provoked Crisis in Cuba" at New York Avenue Presbyterian Church, and closes with a tribute to Dick Gregory's 1976 cross-country run of 3,500 miles — roughly 7 million steps — sustained on fruit juices, vitamins, and water to draw attention to world hunger.

Former Washington, D.C. Mayor Sharon Pratt and her daughter Dr. Aimee Dixon Anthony, director of the documentary series *The Capitol*, joined host Dr. Faye Williams on *Wake Up and Stay Woke* to discuss what the film recovers: that Benjamin Banneker — a free African American whose astronomical knowledge came from a West African tradition — used a photographic memory to reconstruct Pierre L'Enfant's plans after L'Enfant was fired and walked off with the original drawings, and that the capital ended up on the Potomac rather than in Pennsylvania partly because slaveholders feared Pennsylvania's law emancipating any enslaved person held there longer than six months. The episode also featured Talib Muhammad, a Howard-trained engineer and lawyer who described his legal fight after the D.C. Board of Elections gave him 30 minutes to complete 311 pages of petition forms — time the court later confirmed was treated differently than what Democratic candidates received — with a ruling issued just the day before the broadcast. The premiere of *The Capitol* was scheduled for September 9th at the Hirshhorn Museum, with streaming on WETA+ the following day.

Louis Romaine returned from Cuba in May with a delegation organized by Dr. Ron Daniels and the Institute of the Black World — a group that sat down with elected officials, everyday Cubans, and the Cuban president. He traces U.S. hostility toward the island back to the 1854 Ostend Manifesto, in which American diplomats secretly urged President Pierce to seize Cuba by force, fearing it would become an independent Black republic like Haiti. A July 20th State Department report labeling Black internationalism a form of foreign subversion, Romaine argues, runs on the same fear of Black self-determination.

Washington, D.C. spoken word artist and boxer Azaira the Poet describes serving 18 months at Clarksburg Correctional Facility as a teenager, taking up boxing after surviving domestic violence, and performing at Howard University for Children's Mental Health Awareness Day. She performs two poems, including "Trap or Die," which moves through gentrification, absent fathers, and postpartum struggles. Host Dr. Ife Williams leads the conversation throughout on Wake Up and Stay Woke.

Dr. Willie Jolly's grandmother ran a beauty shop in Philadelphia until she died at 88 — doing three heads that morning, a pocket full of money in her smock. On *Wake Up and Stay Woke*, host E. Faye Williams asks Jolly, author of *Rich Is Good, Wealthy Is Better*, to explain the difference between the two: rich is money you earn from what you do, wealthy is money you generate from what you own, usually while you sleep. Jolly lays out five types of wealth — financial, health, relationship, reputational, and intellectual capital — and five money mindsets that range from day-to-day survival to generational planning. He also describes a trust structure he uses with his own family that requires heirs to submit a W-2 each year to receive 5 percent of their earnings as their inheritance payment. Williams, who references her book *This Is Me* and her past run for U.S. Congress in Louisiana, also presses Jolly on voting and what it takes to write a book.

eps.t: Buena Vista Social Club and Beyond
eps.desc:
A Washington judge ordered Kennedy Center trustees to pay jazz musician Chuck Redd $252,000 in legal fees — news Craig Williams broke mid-broadcast on his Morning Brew Classic Jazz Edition. The lawsuit stemmed from the cancellation of Redd's Christmas show, and a "Hands Around the Kennedy Center" rally was set for September 18th.

Williams used Ry Cooder's 1997 Buena Vista Social Club project, later paired with a Wim Wenders film, as an entry point into Cuban jazz's longer history. Roy Hargrove's Crisol band — featuring Chucho Valdés, Gary Bartz, and Russell Malone — shared the program with Mongo Santamaría's "Afro Blue" and "Elephant Pants." Jerry Gonzalez took on Monk's "Misterioso" from *Rumba para Monk*. Gonzalo Rubalcaba played "Transparency" alongside the late Charlie Haden on *Tokyo Adagio*, with further duets pairing Hilario Durán with David Virales.

eps.desc:
Diane Powell, founder and director of Community and Family Builders, wants you to notice the unopened mail, the accumulating boxes from excessive ordering, the forgotten steps for making coffee. These are warning signs of dementia, and she's specific about why Black women need to hear them. African Americans are twice as likely to develop dementia as their white counterparts, two-thirds of those diagnosed are women, and over 7 million people in the U.S. currently live with the disease. Powell gives out the Alzheimer's Association 24/7 hotline number on air.

That same clarity about where people are and what they don't yet know carries into the second conversation. Dr. Hattie Washington — Florida's 2026 Mother of the Year — describes walking onto Norfolk State's campus without having applied, not knowing college required an application or tuition. That story threads into her new book *Happy Motherhood Every Day*, launching on National Relaxation Day, August 15th. Host Faye Williams leads both conversations on *Wake Up and Stay Woke*, Wednesday, August 12, 2026.

Dr. Franklin Malone, president and CEO of 100 Fathers Incorporated, tells *Wake Up and Stay Awake* that the root problem in DC is not violence but fatherlessness. His organization recently held a ceremony at Howard University — the Restorers of the Covenant of Peace — giving posthumous awards to two deceased Council of Elders members. One honoree, Ray Savoy, brought 100 Fathers into DC schools including Ballou, Phelps, Woodson, Anacostia, and Friendship Collegiate, and taught young men golf at Langston Golf Course.

The hour, hosted by Dr. E. Fay Williams and airing during a station fundraising drive, also turns to Howard University itself. Dr. Robert Cosby, Assistant Dean for Administration at the Howard University School of Social Work, explains the school's dual master's programs — an on-campus "Flagship" and an online "Starship" — as it marks its 90th year. He currently teaches a doctoral course tracing social welfare history from 1619 forward, drawing on Nikole Hannah-Jones's work.

Danielle Smith's granddaughter stood before Representatives Clyburn, Jasmine Crockett, and Melanie Campbell at the Congressional Black Caucus — one example of how Smith's Baltimore chapter of Black Women for Positive Change pushes young people directly in front of elected officials. The chapter's Month of Nonviolence program has run poetry cyphers, peace circles, and an essay contest where participants wrote on changing community violence culture and competed for donated laptops.

Dr. Franklin Malone of 100 Fathers brings a complementary perspective. Named the number-one family support organization in the DMV by the *Washington Informer*, 100 Fathers holds an annual Healing and Restoring the Soul of Our Community conference at Howard University. Malone announces the August 2nd Restorers of the Covenant of Peace Awards ceremony at the Howard University School of Social Work, honoring community members including parents who lost children to gun violence and returned to schools to work against it. Host Faye Williams leads the conversation on Wake Up, Stay Woke.

people.name: DJ Zee-Lion
bio: DJ Zee-Lion is Ziah Ayubu, a Rasta man, musician, and DJ who serves as the host of Kulcha Shak on WPFW. Born in St. Vincent and the Grenadines, Ziah grew up during a time when Rastas were frequently targeted and harassed for their way of life, an experience that shaped his deep commitment to culture and community. He brings this perspective to the airwaves every Saturday, where he and his co-host and wife, Sista Kim Bey, curate an eclectic mix of music intended to bridge the cultural gap between Africa and its global diaspora.

Ziah's journey with the station began after he moved to the D.C. area and found himself drawn to WPFW for its unique style of music and essential information. Already established as a musician, he joined the programming team in 2016 after a friend informed him the station was looking for a reggae host. For Ziah, radio is a vital tool for connection; he believes that music is the healing of the nation and uses his program to represent the full spectrum of sounds from across the African diaspora.

An accomplished artist beyond the studio, Ziah is the founder of the Proverbs Reggae Band and has released two albums along with several singles. His musical contributions have earned him significant recognition, including being a five-time DC Reggae Award winner and a DC Wammie Award winner. He has performed as a main act regionally, opened for numerous international reggae artists, and took second place during Caribbean night at the legendary Apollo Theater.

In his life outside of music and broadcasting, Ziah remains dedicated to the well-being of his neighbors. He is passionate about working within the community to help people access and understand natural foods, herbs, and supplements. Guided by the principle to think globally and act locally, Ziah encourages the WPFW community to stay involved in local efforts and support one another to create lasting progress.

eps.desc: DJ Z Lion is solo this week on *Kulcha Shak*, with co-host Kim Bey away, steering through reggae, R&B, soca, and African music. Two DC-area artists get the spotlight early: "Soulmate," produced by Danny Queen with Jerome McCall and Lauren White on vocals, and Big Chest DC's go-go-flavored "She's Always in My Hair." The playlist moves from Junior Marvin and Pressure Busspipe to Jackie Wilson, Marvin Gaye, and Frankie Beverly and Maze — and mid-show, Everett called in to wish his wife Marie Robertson Green a happy birthday, the couple married 66 years.

Steel Pulse's "Heart of Stone" opens the show, and that choice sets the terms for what follows: two hours in which DJ Zee-Lion and Kim Bey pursue their stated mission of "musically bridging the cultural gap between Africa and the diaspora." Kulcha Shak moves through reggae, R&B, and soul, with sets drawing on Morgan Heritage, Bushman, Chalice, and Elaine Brown before the back stretch loosens its reggae roots into R&B and touches of jazz, closing out on "Sunny Gets Blue" and Sly Stone's "Stand.
